news.title: New 2028 presidential frontrunner has emerged on a key prediction market site
news.text:
Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is now the frontrunner to become the 2028 Democratic presidential nominee, according to Polymarket odds, marking the first time she has led the pack. 

As of Wednesday evening, 21 percent of traders backed the New York progressive, who was trailed by California Governor Gavin Newsom at 17 percent. On rival prediction site Kalshi, the results were the same, with Ocasio-Cortez narrowly topping Newsom. 

Meanwhile, conventional political polls still put former Vice President Kamala Harris at the top spot, with Newsom in second and AOC in a distant fourth. 

Ocasio-Cortez has not announced a formal presidential bid, nor has she sworn one off. Right now she’s focused on helping Democrats win the midterms, she recently told The Independent.

“I think my main focus is really genuinely just the midterms right now, and we have to make sure that we win this majority,” she said.

Ocasio-Cortez recently made headlines for detailing the process of freezing her eggs on social media and reflecting on the precarious state of women’s healthcare in America.

“In the political context that we're in, in an administration that is dedicated to politicizing women’s bodies and taking our choices away from us and punishing us around decisions to be pregnant or not be pregnant — and, frankly, this administration has made pregnancy more dangerous than probably at any point in the last 30 plus years — we’re gonna take our power back,” she told her followers. 

She also generated considerable discussion in political circles for branding 2020-era “woke” ideas “crazy,” reflecting that while many of the social justice-focused discussions of that era were “fruitful,” the "rhetoric in that time is not rhetoric that we would use today.” 

An AOC 2028 bid would be the latest test of whether Democrats will move further to the left, in line with rising Democratic socialists and progressives such as New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, or whether the party will tack back to the center.

In many ways, the party is still reeling from the 2024 election, where Harris replaced President Joe Biden in the late stages of the race and lost to Donald Trump, despite the Republican campaigning under a cloud of lawsuits and government investigations. 

Considerable divides remain in the party over issues including healthcare, U.S. support for Israel and immigration. 

The Democrats are projected to retake at least the House in the midterms, according to polling, on the back of high gas prices and an unpopular war in Iran.
news.summary: Democrats still reeling from the 2024 election, where Harris replaced President Joe Biden in the late stages of the race and lost to Donald Trump
news.author: Josh Marcus

news.title: Jen Psaki Said It Out Loud: Party Leaders ‘Really Selected’ Nominees
news.text:
Jen Psaki may have just said one of the most revealing things I've heard from a former Democratic White House official in years.

The former Biden White House press secretary, who now hosts The Briefing with Jen Psaki on MS Now, was discussing Democrat primaries when she casually acknowledged how the system once worked:

"Party leadership really selected the nominees."

Jen Psaki admits on MSNBC that Democratic Party leadership used to “SELECT” the nominees, and nobody was allowed to say it out loud until now.PSAKI: “We both remember well when party leadership really selected the nominees.”“Now, you would never say it that way exactly, but… pic.twitter.com/puZEN4FVvX— The Vigilant Fox 🦊 (@VigilantFox) August 12, 2026

Psaki added that nobody would have described it quite so openly at the time.

Listen to and read her words again: Party leadership really selected the nominees.

Americans should hear that sentence everywhere because it comes from somebody who spent years inside Democratic politics, including senior communications jobs in the Obama and Biden administrations.

Psaki wasn't some outsider guessing about smoke-filled rooms; she worked in the rooms.

Bernie Sanders supporters learned a painful version of the lesson in 2016. Leaked internal emails exposed hostility toward Sanders inside the Democratic National Committee during his primary battle with Hillary Clinton.

The DNC eventually issued what it called a "deep and sincere apology" to Sanders and his supporters for the conduct revealed in those messages.

“On behalf of everyone at the DNC, we want to offer a deep and sincere apology to Senator Sanders, his supporters, and the entire Democratic Party for the inexcusable remarks made over email. These comments do not reflect the values of the DNC or our steadfast commitment to neutrality during the nominating process. The DNC does not — and will not — tolerate disrespectful language exhibited toward our candidates. Individual staffers have also rightfully apologized for their comments, and the DNC is taking appropriate action to ensure it never happens again.“We are embarking on a convention today that — thanks to the great efforts of Secretary Clinton, her team, Senator Sanders, his team, and the entire Democratic Party — will show a forward-thinking and optimistic vision for America, as compared to the dark and pessimistic vision that the GOP presented last week in Cleveland. Our focus is on electing Hillary Clinton, Tim Kaine and Democrats across the country, thanks to Democratic Party that is strong, unified, and poised for victory in November.”

Clinton still won more primary votes and pledged delegates, so I won't claim somebody secretly changed ballots to steal the nomination from Sanders. The documented problem was party neutrality.

Democrat officials themselves apologized after internal communications showed the supposedly neutral organization wasn't behaving very neutrally.

Then came 2024.

Joe Biden won the Democratic presidential primaries and dropped out in July. Democrat voters never received another presidential primary in which they could choose his replacement.

Kamala Harris became the only candidate who qualified for the DNC's virtual roll-call ballot after 3,923 delegates signed petitions supporting her.

A few days later, 4,567 delegates voted for Harris, giving her 99% support among participating delegates. She became the Democratic presidential nominee without ever winning a presidential primary for the job in 2024.

The next steps in the nominating process include the certification of the roll call by the Convention Secretary Jason Rae, and the acceptance of the nomination by Vice President Harris and her running mate, certified by DNCC Chair Minyon Moore. Delegates will then celebrate the nomination through a celebratory Roll Call at the in-person Convention, gaveled in by DNC Chair Jaime Harrison and DNCC Chair Minyon Moore.Statement from DNC Chair Jaime Harrison and DNCC Chair Minyon Moore:“With the support of 99% of all participating delegates in the virtual roll call, Vice President Harris has historic momentum at her back as we embark on the final steps in officially certifying her as our Party’s nominee. We thank the thousands of delegates from all across the country who took seriously their responsibility throughout this process to make their voices – and the voices of their communities – heard. As we prepare to certify the nomination alongside Convention Secretary Rae, we know that we are all a part of an important piece of history. Soon, it will be time to come together in Chicago, where we will celebrate together and make clear to the American people that the Democratic Party is the party of freedom, of democracy, of rights, and of the people.” 

Now Psaki says party leaders once "really selected the nominees."

Maybe Democrats will argue she was merely describing an older political era when endorsements, donors, and party bosses carried greater influence.

Her explanation still deserves attention because 2016 and 2024 make the subject anything but ancient history.

Democrats spent years presenting themselves as guardians of democracy while warning Americans that Republicans threatened voters' voices. Meanwhile, their own recent history contains a national party apologizing for misconduct toward one presidential candidate and later nominating another candidate whom Democrat primary voters never selected for president.

Psaki's sentence belongs outside the cable-news echo chamber.

news.title: The town making missiles for Trump
news.text:
If you're not conservative, don't come here': The town making missiles for Trump

As one local puts it, there's a "church on every street" of the Appalchian community of Kingsport, in the US state of Tennessee.

Christianity reigns supreme in this working-class area. Above downtown's historic Lamplight Theatre, a sign proclaims "Jesus first in all things".

And while more than 300 area churches may be providing spiritual sustenance to this town of 58,000 people, there's another institution that supplies it with economic nourishment.

The Holston Army Ammunition Plant churns out explosives used in Patriot missiles, warheads and other heavy weaponry in the midst of the country's costly and prolonged war with Iran.

The war, and its knock-on effects on everything from gas to groceries, has led to a steep decline in President Donald Trump's approval ratings. Recent polling has placed his approval at an historic low of 32% - down 14% from when he first took office in January 2025 - with many Republican respondents citing disillusionment with the president's policies.

The two big drags on the president's popularity are the cost of living and the Iran War, with one bleeding into the other. The conflict has caused gas prices in the US to spike to above $4 a gallon, a painful hike to any US business that relies on transport.

But in Kingsport, support for the president approaches an almost-religious fervor. The city voted overwhelmingly for Trump in all three of his elections. So did wider Tennessee, a Republican state for more than 25 years.

When it comes to the Iran conflict, most residents either outright support the military action or rationalise the war's necessity - despite Trump's repeated campaign promise of "no more wars".

"If he can stop anyone from having a nuclear bomb, then I'm for it," says Pam Robinson, 65, who spent 20 years working at the local chemical plant.

David Carter, a bearded veteran who plays Santa Claus at Christmastime, says "the whole reason we go over there, and we keep everything under control there, is [so that] we don't have it on our doorstep."

Others are more blunt.

"Honestly, I think we should turn them into a parking lot and don't worry about it anymore," says veteran James Camper, 63, wearing a Trump lanyard around his neck as he exits a discount grocery.

Veterans account for around 10% of the region's population, and many other households have active duty family members.

Robinson, a staunch Christian and independent voter who says her faith informs her candidate choices, believes the remote nature of the war may be preventing local people from being more upset with Trump.

"Let me say this: If it was hand-to-hand and more people were getting killed, people would be banging the doors down," she says.

Kingsport's position as a main munitions manufacturer - with Holston standing as the only domestic supplier of some essential explosive and propellant components - gives its residents a unique perspective when it comes to the war in Iran.

The plant employs around 1,000 people and is just one of many sprawling industrial complexes standing out starkly from the lush Appalachian Mountain landscape.

"The plant's going to be open regardless of whether we're at war or whether we're not," says Daniel Overstreet, 53, standing next to his Harley Davidson in downtown Kingsport. "It is what it is."

He believes Trump and the administration are "doing a great job" but there are "too many people trying to fight him."

"[He said] he would get the gas prices under control, and they were for a while," says Overstreet. "He said he was gonna get food prices down, but he has no control over that. The president is basically a puppet for Congress and the Senate.

"His hands are tied, to a certain extent."

It's not that people here don't complain about high gas and food prices, inflation and other economic woes - it's just they don't blame Trump for any of it.

"He's done good on some things; I think he needs to check his advisers and see on some things," says Robinson. "I think he's advised wrong on some things."

It was Trump himself, however, who announced his decision to strike Iran in February 2026 following failed negotiations. In an eight-minute video posted to social media, he said "the objective is to defend the American people by eliminating imminent threats from the Iranian regime" - and claimed Iran "will never have a nuclear weapon."

Evangelist William Bogle, 75, voted for Trump every time he ran and believes the president is "doing a good job" - even though his wife "has to stretch a grocery dollar until, you know, it's big as a bedsheet".

Trump is "just gonna have to do a little bit better in some things than he's doing right now," he says.

"I know he wants the country to prosper."

This stalwart support reflects a deeper truth sometimes hidden in the polling headlines. Although Trump has lost favour among more traditional Republicans and independent voters, his base - who self-identify with his "Make America Great Again" mantra - remains much more steadfast in backing him.

So while much of the US watches to see how much Trump's sliding popularity may damage Republicans in November's midterm elections, here in the Bible Belt, sometimes red is the only option.

As voters turned out last week for local elections, the ballot included a single Democratic candidate. Of the county commission's 11 districts, seven featured only Republicans running, with some unopposed.

Many say they can't and won't cross party lines for moral reasons, citing abortion as the single biggest deciding factor, with opposition to socialism and "woke" issues too hard for them to ignore.

Those fears outweigh any personal criticisms they may have, says David Carter, 66, a grandfather and Christian as well as a veteran.

Trump needs to humble himself more, he concedes, but Carter would only consider a candidate who "supports the morals" of the population. That means opposing abortion, for example.

Those who hold more liberal views exist in Kingsport, but they're vastly in the minority and less vocal.

Piercing artist Adam Teague, 44, is a gay, heavily-tattooed Democrat working in downtown Kingsport.

"Before Trump took office, I was wearing, like, rainbow shirts and everything," says Teague, who was raised Baptist. "I kind of toned it down, just to feel safer."

Trump was triumphant in the 2024 election in part because of his ability to attract a diverse coalition including people of all ages and races. But while his Maga supporters are sticking by him, polling suggests that many young people who helped get him over the line against Kamala Harris are now disillusioned.

Mary Herron, 21, who is leaving a boutique cupcake shop with two friends, has noticed a difference in attitudes amongst her contemporaries.

"I am seeing a shift in the support … that's kind of rare around here," says Herron, a student who works part-time. "But I've seen a handful of people who have been like, 'Oh yeah, well, I voted for him, and now I'm not with him anymore."

Trump first entered politics when the women were in middle school, says her friend Emily Villalpando, 21. "So a lot of the people that we grew up with kind of just adopted their parents' views.

"And so now that we're growing up, we're having more responsibilities," says Villalpando, who's studying biomedical science and wants to be a doctor. "The economy affects us a lot more."

The three college students - their friend Caden Bayless makes up the trio - cite women's rights and heavy-handed immigration agents as major concerns, but they are sceptical of major attitude or voting shifts in the region. 

Bayless said she is hopeful the younger generation can make a change, but "given where we live … it would be a very difficult change."

Bogle, summing up the Kingsport region, inadvertently speaks to their fears.

"We live in a great place, and if you're not conservative, don't come here," the preacher says. "Because you wouldn't be a good fit. But if you're conservative, come here, and we'll embrace you."

He'll be praying for Trump, he says, as will the more moderate Robinson.

"All you can do is pray for your leaders, and God will give you what you want in the end," she says.
news.author: Sheila Flynn

news.title: Trump sued over sale of access to Truth Social posts
news.text:
The lawsuit by two US media groups stated that the Truth Social scheme was 'extraordinary, corrupt and unconstitutional'. (Reuters pic)
NEW YORK: Two US media groups on Wednesday sued president Donald Trump over his move to charge for early access to his often market-moving Truth Social posts.
The lawsuit, filed in New York by The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation, states that the scheme is "extraordinary, corrupt and unconstitutional".
Subscribers to the paid service are supposed to get almost instantaneous access to Trump's messages on the Truth Social platform - crucial seconds ahead of the general public.
The billionaire Republican often uses the platform to announce huge news, ranging from developments in the Iran war to trade tariffs, all of which can instantly send market values tumbling or soaring.
Early access to the service can cost up to US$100,000 per month, or US$60,000 per month if users commit to three years, according to Wednesday's lawsuit.
"This scheme is profoundly corrupt. The President stands to gain financially by giving 'market-moving' government information to those who are willing and able to pay his personal company," a court filing says.
Trump Media & Technology Group, the company running the platform, has dismissed concerns over the product, which is called Truth API and was first unveiled in mid-July.
Calls for probe
The Intercept, a nonprofit US news outlet, and Freedom of the Press Foundation, which operates a database tracking Truth Social posts, argue that the paid service hinders their ability to properly cover Trump.
"Timely access to the President's posts is critical for both groups," the filing states, asking the court to declare Truth API as unlawful and block future posts.
Several Democratic lawmakers have called for a probe into the service by the Securities and Exchange Commission, which regulates US markets.
Trump Media interim CEO Kevin McGurn said this week that Truth API is already generating revenue with 10 customer agreements signed, though he did not identify the clients.
The Wall Street Journal has reported that trading companies were among the first to subscribe to the service.
On Monday, Trump Media posted a ten-fold jump in losses for the second quarter of 2026, linked to declines in values of its digital assets.
Trump, like his close relatives, is alleged to have made billions of dollars in his second White House term through cryptocurrency ventures, property deals, stock trades and payouts from lawsuits.
Forbes, a financial media outlet, has estimated that Trump's net worth shot up from US$2.3 billion to US$6.5 billion since 2024, when he won the election over Kamala Harris.
news.summary: Early access to the service can cost up to US$100,000 per month, or US$60,000 monthly with a three-year commitment.

news.title: Democrat and Republican Voter Turnout Compared in Six Key Primary States
news.text: Democratic turnout surged in the primary elections in several key states like Georgia, Michigan and Texas ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. As the midterms inch closer, Democrats are increasingly optimistic about their chances of winning key races across the country. Historically, the party in the White House loses seats in the midterms, and President Donald Trump’s declining approval rating has fueled Democrats’ hopes of expanding the battleground. Democrats also see signs of heightened enthusiasm among their voters, including higher primary turnout in key states, though some experts do not view primary turnout as predictive. Across the board, turnout has risen during the Trump era as more and more Americans are engaged in politics. Numerous factors can influence primary turnout, including voter motivation, as well as the number of contentious primaries each party has; if one party has more contested primaries, they may see higher turnout. So far, Democrats are seeing a rise in turnout in several key states they are hoping to win in November. What Does Primary Turnout Signal for the Midterms? Grant Davis Reeher, professor of political science at Syracuse University, told Newsweek it’s normally difficult to conclude much about a general election based on primary turnout. “However, it does appear that Democrats are enjoying more intense interest and enthusiasm among their primary voters than Republicans. This reflects the heightened media and public interest generated by the candidates on the Left on the Democratic side, and some ambivalence and uncertainty on the Republican side,” he said. It’s still an “open question” whether that enthusiasm gap will extend to the general election, he said. “Whether that enthusiasm gap extends to the general election is an open question. Republicans may become motivated to counter the Leftward drift of the Democrats. But in any case, none of the other indicators suggest anything good for Republicans in the mid-terms,” he said. Democrats’ high primary turnout does signal enthusiasm among their voters, but that’s something they’ll need to maintain through the general election, Todd Belt, director of the Political Management Program at George Washington University, told Newsweek on Wednesday. “Democrats are angry and highly motivated to take on not just Trump, but many want to take on the Democratic establishment in DC,” he said. He noted that Democrats may still have a difficult time working to “heal the wounds” of some of their most contested primaries, and that may be a more difficult task in cases where moderates win because progressive voters “care more about ideological purity than compromise.” Republicans may be facing lower turnout because they have fewer competitive races, and they may be less enthusiastic about their chances in November, he said. “Two key variables tend to drive turnout: the perceived closeness of the race and the perceived importance of the office. For Democrats, these races are extremely important because they want to nominate candidates to the general election who will take on the Trump administration,” he said. Some politics experts have been skeptical that there is any connection between turnout in a primary and the eventual results of a general election, especially as uncontested or uncompetitive primaries can drive down turnout. Nate Silver wrote in a Substack post that Democratic turnout surged in Texas earlier this year but noted he is not one to believe that necessarily means Democrats are favored to flip the seat. “I’m not a big believer in primary turnout being predictive of general election outcomes, but this is nevertheless a big number for Democrats in a red state,” he wrote. Republican National Press Secretary Natalie Baldassarre told Newsweek that Republicans are “confident voters will turn out to protect and expand our majorities” as Trump is “barnstorming the country touting his America First agenda that’s lowered taxes, secured our border, and made our streets safe.” “It’s common sense versus communism at the ballot box this November, and our candidates are on offense to ensure Americans reject Democrats’ plans to turn our country into a third-world dystopia,” she said. A Democratic National Committee spokesperson told Newsweek that primary turnout “shows that our grassroots organizing is paying off across the country.” “At a time when voters are ready to turn the page on Republicans’ harmful cost-spiking agenda, Americans are energized, fired up, and ready to elect Democrats who will make life more affordable, protect healthcare, tackle Republicans’ corruption, and put working families first,” the spokesperson said. How Voter Turnout Compares in Six Key States Georgia The nation’s latest battleground is going to be the site of some of the most competitive primaries of the midterms. Although it backed Trump by about 2 points in 2024, Democrats are hopeful about their chances in the state this time around. Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff is up for reelection, while the governor race between former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat, and Republican businessman Rick Jackson is viewed as a toss-up. Both parties had highly competitive governor primaries in May, but Democrats saw higher turnout on their side. In the Republican primary, there were a total of 933,817 votes cast, according to the Georgia secretary of state’s office. That compares to 1,081,811 votes cast on the Democratic side. That’s a notable shift from the 2018 midterms, the last time both parties had a primary in the governor race, when 607,441 votes were cast in the GOP primary and 555,089 votes were cast in the Democratic primary. Iowa Democrats are also hoping to make a comeback in Iowa, a former swing state that has shifted toward Republicans over recent cycles. Iowa backed Trump by 13 points in 2024, but it backed former President Barack Obama in his 2008 and 2012 runs. In the governor race, Democratic state Auditor Rob Sand is facing Republican Zach Lahn. In the Senate race, Republican Representative Ashley Hinson and Democratic state Representative Josh Turek are running. Sand's primary was uncontested, and Republicans outvoted Democrats in the Senate primary, according to the Iowa secretary of state’s office. There were 206,786 votes cast in the Republican Senate primary, compared to 192,136 votes in the Democratic primary. For comparison, there were 198,858 Republican ballots and 158,745 Democratic ballots cast in 2022. In 2018, there were 105,183 Republican ballots cast, compared to 182,736 Democratic ballots cast. Democrats had several competitive races for governor and in congressional races, while Republican races were less competitive. Maine The Maine Senate race is a top target for Democrats, as they hope to topple longtime GOP Senator Susan Collins, who has won reelection in the past due to her personal popularity and bipartisan image, despite the state’s Democratic lean. Maine backed former Vice President Kamala Harris by about 7 points in 2024. Collins ran unopposed in the Republican primary, and just over 216,000 votes were cast in the Democratic primary. However, the party’s chosen candidate, Graham Platner, withdrew from the race amid sexual abuse allegations, which he has denied. Troy Jackson, the former president of the Maine Senate, was selected as the new nominee during a convention. But both parties had competitive governor races. Democrat Hannah Pingree, the former speaker of the Maine House of Representatives, and Republican Bobby Charles emerged victorious from their respective primaries. In total, there were 217,493 votes cast in the Democratic primary and 129,084 votes cast in the Republican primary, according to the Maine secretary of state’s office. That marks an increase for Democrats compared to their last contested primary in 2018, when there were 126,139 ballots cast. Republicans have not had contested governor primaries in recent cycles. Michigan Democrats and Republicans both had a competitive primary in the governor race, though only Democrats had a competitive Senate primary. Michigan went to Trump by fewer than 2 points in 2024, and it’s viewed as one of the most evenly divided battlegrounds across the country. In the Senate race, progressive public health official Abdul El-Sayed is facing former Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican. Democratic Senator Gary Peters opted to retire at the end of his term. In the governor race, Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and Republican Representative John James are running. In the governor primary, there were 1,494,915 ballots cast for Democrats and 929,475 ballots cast for Republicans, according to the Michigan Secretary of State office. In the Senate primary, there were 1,528,954 ballots cast for Democrats and 880,519 cast for Rogers in the GOP primary, though he ran unopposed, so the race was simply not competitive. There was an open Senate race in 2024, which saw 933,844 votes cast in the Democratic primary and 879,569 votes cast in the Republican primary. In 2018, the last time both parties had an open governor race, there were 989,576 Republican ballots cast and 1,131,447 Democratic ballots cast. Texas Democrats saw a particularly strong primary turnout surge in Texas, a historically Republican state that has the potential to become competitive in November. The Senate race, in which Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic state legislator James Talarico are competing, is especially competitive. Forecasters like the Cook Political Report favor Republicans in the governor race, where Governor Greg Abbott is facing Democratic legislator Gina Hinojosa. There were 2,166,910 votes cast in the Republican Senate primary, compared to 2,319,187 ballots cast in the Democratic primary. In the governor primary, there were 2,156,879 ballots cast on the Republican side and 2,203,671 on the Democratic side. In 2024, there were 2,239,958 ballots cast in the Republican Senate primary, compared to 967,503 ballots cast on the Democratic side. There was also a notable gap in 2018, when Democrats had more competitive primaries than Republicans but still significantly lagged in turnout. There were 1,549,573 votes cast in the Senate Republican primary, compared to 1,042,914 votes cast in the Democratic primary. In the governor race that year, there were 1,549,006 votes cast for Republicans and 1,022,558 ballots cast for Democrats. Wisconsin Wisconsin is another evenly divided state that narrowly went to Trump in 2024; in fact, it was the closest state in the most recent presidential race, and has a competitive gubernatorial race this year, as Democratic Governor Tony Evers retires. Voters in the state cast their ballots on Tuesday, picking Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley and Republican Representative Tom Tiffany as the Democratic and Republican nominees, respectively. While the Democratic primary against state legislator Francesca Hong was very competitive, the Republican primary was not, with turnout being down for the party. According to The New York Times, there were 798,018 Democratic ballots cast compared to 490,819 ballots cast with more than 95 percent reporting on Wednesday. In 2022, Republicans outvoted Democrats in the Senate primaries, with 672,975 votes being cast in the Republican primary and 501,089 ballots cast in the Democratic primary. In 2018, there were 537,719 votes cast in the Democratic governor primary, compared to 455,966 votes cast in the Republican primary. The Republican primary, in which then-Governor Scott Walker ran, was not competitive. What Happens Next Many of these races are expected to be competitive in November. Here is a look at how the Cook Political Report classifies each of the elections. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Democratic turnout surged in states like Georgia and Texas in this year's midterm primaries.
news.author: Andrew Stanton

news.title: Fox News Poll: New matchup, same result: Maine Senate race stays locked
news.text: Maine voters are weighing concerns about both U.S. Senate candidates, with anxieties over Republican incumbent Senator Susan Collins' ties to President Donald Trump outpacing concerns about Democratic challenger Troy Jackson's progressive alignment, according to a Fox News statewide poll released Wednesday. Collins has represented Maine in the Senate since 1997, winning her fifth term in 2020 by nearly 9 percentage points. The new survey shows more than half of Maine voters, 55%, are concerned her voting record aligns with President Trump too often, while fewer, 43%, are worried Jackson is too close to the Democratic Socialist movement. FOX NEWS POLL: GOP DIVISIONS SHAPE TEXAS SENATE RACE By a 14-point margin, more independents are worried Collins is too close to Trump than are concerned Jackson is too close to the Democratic Socialists. Jackson, a fifth-generation logger from Allagash and former president of the Maine Senate, replaced Graham Platner as the Democratic nominee in July after Platner withdrew amid an assault allegation. Jackson’s candidacy makes the contest more of a referendum on Collins: 61% of his supporters say their vote is mainly against Collins, up from 48% when Platner was the opponent. Only 36% say they’re voting for Jackson, down from Platner’s 50%. FOX NEWS POLL: DEMOCRATIC ENTHUSIASM SHAPES NORTH CAROLINA SENATE RACE The contrast is even clearer for Collins: 71% of her backers say they’re voting mainly for her, up from 53% in June. Just 27% are voting against Jackson, down from 45% when it was Platner. Despite a major change in the Democratic ticket, the survey finds the Maine Senate race remains competitive. Jackson tops Collins by 2 percentage points, 48-46%, well within the survey’s margin of sampling error. In June, Collins was ahead of Platner by 3 points. Since then, Collins’ support is down 4 points, while Jackson does 1 point better than Platner. Among the subgroup of voters who rate themselves a 10-out-of-10 on certainty to vote, Jackson’s edge increases to 4 points (50-46%). By an 8-point margin, more of those backing Collins say their choice is locked in. One in five Jackson supporters say they may change their mind before voting. Roughly 9 in 10 partisans back their respective candidate, while independents narrowly prefer Jackson. Jackson’s best groups include liberals, women with a college degree, and those under age 35. He also leads among men under age 45 and those in union households. He’s favored by women by 4 points, while men are evenly divided. Collins’ biggest support comes from conservatives, White evangelical Christians, men ages 45 and up, and voters without a college degree. She’s also ahead among rural and married voters. Compared to Platner’s numbers in June, Jackson mostly holds steady with key constituencies including women, voters with a college degree, and suburban voters, while making gains among those under age 45 (12 points better than Platner). At the same time, Collins’ previous 10-point advantage among men has evaporated. Almost all MAGA Republicans back Collins, but that drops to three-quarters among non-MAGA Republicans (nearly one in five non-MAGA back Jackson). For Jackson, almost all supporters of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) movement back him, but that falls to two-thirds among non-DSA Democrats and independents. "Replacing Platner with Jackson has allowed two other factors to assert themselves — opposition to President Trump and a desire for change," says Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who conducts Fox News polls with Democrat Chris Anderson. "The race remains close and I’d never count Collins out, but you have to give a slight edge to the Democrats here." FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS WANT MAJOR CHANGE AMID ECONOMIC AND POLITICAL DISCONTENT Collins is the only GOP senator running for reelection this year from a state Trump lost in 2024 (former Vice President Kamala Harris won the Pine Tree State by 7 points). Meanwhile, Trump’s personal favorable rating is underwater by 20 points (39% favorable vs. 59% unfavorable). Democrats view Maine as a must-win seat in their effort to take control of the Senate. Inflation remains the top issue in Maine, as one-third say it will be the most important factor in deciding their Senate vote. The other priorities are immigration/border security, healthcare, and political divisions within the country. Part of Jackson’s lead is built on the support of the 4 in 10 who say they’re falling behind financially, where he leads by 29 points. Ratings of Collins are unfavorable by 10 points (44% vs. 54%), which is more negative than in June when her ratings were underwater by 3 points (47-50%). Jackson’s favorable rating is positive by a single point (47% favorable vs. 46% unfavorable). Views of both Senate candidates are more positive than those of their respective political parties. Voters who hold negative opinions of both candidates prefer Jackson by 3 points in the horse race, while those viewing both major parties unfavorably back him by 22 points. Pingree’s personal favorable rating is net positive by 15 points (52% favorable vs. 37% unfavorable). Charles’ rating is underwater by 6 (36% vs. 42%), while 23% are unfamiliar with him. Bennett is even less well known, with 52% unable to rate him. news.title: AOC Takes Lead Over Gavin Newsom in 2028 Odds for First Time
news.text: Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has overtaken California Governor Gavin Newsom in prediction market odds for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination for the first time, according to data from Polymarket highlighted Wednesday by the political-tracking account InteractivePolls. The market showed Ocasio-Cortez at 18 percent, narrowly ahead of Newsom at 17 percent. Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff ranked third at 16 percent, while former Vice President Kamala Harris stood at 8 percent. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro each came in at 5 percent. The shift marks a notable moment in the still-early race to shape the Democratic field ahead of the 2028 election. While neither Ocasio-Cortez nor Newsom has officially launched a presidential campaign, both have long been viewed as potential contenders representing different wings of the Democratic Party. Ocasio-Cortez is a leading progressive voice in Congress, while Newsom has emerged as one of the party's most prominent establishment figures and has frequently been mentioned as a future White House candidate. Prediction markets are not scientific opinion polls and do not measure voter support directly. Instead, they reflect how traders are wagering on future political outcomes. As a result, market movements are often driven by news events, perceptions of candidate viability, and speculation about who is most likely to run and ultimately secure the nomination. The latest move is particularly significant because Newsom had been viewed as the front-runner in many early discussions about the 2028 Democratic race. Ocasio-Cortez's rise suggests traders increasingly see her as a serious contender for the nomination, even if the primary season remains more than two years away. Kalshi, another political prediction market, is still ranking Newsom as the favorite, with Ocasio-Cortez in second place. How AOC's Rise Reflects the Democratic Party's Divide Ocasio-Cortez's move to the top of the Polymarket standings is likely to intensify discussion about the Democratic Party's ideological direction heading into 2028. The New York congresswoman has become one of the country's most recognizable progressive leaders, championing policies such as Medicare for All, aggressive climate action and expanded social programs. Newsom, by contrast, is often viewed as a leading establishment Democrat with executive experience governing the nation's most populous state. The emergence of Ocasio-Cortez, Newsom and Ossoff as the top three contenders in prediction markets suggests traders see a competitive battle between different wings and generations of the party. While the eventual field remains uncertain, the latest odds indicate there is no clear consensus favorite among Democratic observers nearly two years before the nomination contest begins. Why Prediction Markets Are Drawing Attention Political prediction markets have increasingly become a closely watched barometer of campaign sentiment because they update in real time as traders react to news and political developments. Unlike traditional polls, which survey voters, markets such as Polymarket reflect where participants are willing to place money on future outcomes. Still, analysts caution against treating prediction markets as forecasts of election results. Market prices can shift rapidly based on media attention, emerging narratives or speculation about potential candidates entering the race. The fact that Ocasio-Cortez now leads on Polymarket while Newsom remains ahead on Kalshi highlights how different prediction platforms can produce different snapshots of the political landscape. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Anna Commander and Sam Wilson.
news.summary: Political prediction markets have increasingly become a closely watched barometer of campaign sentiment as they update.

Marty O'Donnell running as a Republican for Congress in Nevada’s 3rd Congressional District, but there is way more happening behinds the scenes than the typical congressional run.

'Propaganda from leftist supporters ...'

Tarnished halo

O'Donnell is considered video game royalty after he composed the legendary theme song for the Halo series, which has cumulatively sold more than 80 million copies.

That is why O'Donnell makes appearances at popular conventions, and this was no different for SacAnime, in Sacramento in September.

O'Donnell said online that he was set to make a 25th anniversary appearance at SacAnime to celebrate the game, but was told he is no longer invited due to staff at the event voicing concerns about their safety.

While it isn't clear what the event is referring to in particular, the cancellation comes following O'Donnell being put under the spotlight by Democrats last month.

news.title: Union Boss At Center Of Warring Socialist Factions In Battle For Control
news.text:
The leftist president of the United Auto Workers seems to be caught between a rock and a hard place as a more extreme faction takes aim at him and his socialist supporters.

President Shawn Fain took the reins of United Auto Workers (UAW) in 2023 after narrowly winning its first direct presidential election. He promised to end corruption in the union and make it a more bottom-up system, but some rank-and-file members have since shown opposition to his leadership.

The president ran with support from a now-defunct union reform group founded in part by socialists, the Unite All Workers for Democracy (UAWD), which contributed to his successful election. However the World Socialist Web Site (WSWS), has pushed back on Fain, emphasizing the divide between him and its preferred UAW presidential candidate, socialist Will Lehman, in the 2026 UAW election.

WSWS claimed that the online UAW presidential candidate forum held July 30 “laid bare the gulf between” Lehman, who it called a “rank-and-file Mack Trucks worker,” and the other candidates such as Fain “who are contending for control of an apparatus sitting atop $1.25 billion in net assets.”

In an article about the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) grand jury investigation of Fain, WSWS claimed that a federal monitor’s findings about the union boss “underscore the significance” of Lehman’s campaign, as he is “running on a platform of abolishing the bureaucracy and transferring power to the rank and file.”

With the 2026 UAW election around the corner, a federal grand jury has been probing claims about Fain that he abused his office as president to financially benefit his fiancée and her sister.

Fain claims that the federal monitor’s claims are completely false and the monitor has a “political grudge” against him, according to the Detroit Free Press. However, the WSWS believes that the federal monitor has actually “gone out of his way to prop him up.”

Some Democrats are looking to Fain to run for president, but he has not indicated an intent to do that yet, according to Politico.

The UAW, the WSWS and Lehman each did not respond to the Daily Caller News Foundation’s requests for comment. (RELATED: Democratic Socialists Of America Supporters Have This In Common)

I'm announcing my campaign today for president of the UAW.I'm a Mack Trucks worker from Macungie, PA.My campaign will mobilize the rank and file to1) abolish the corrupt UAW bureaucracy2) put all power in the hands of workersClass struggle, not class collaboration! pic.twitter.com/QceHTUcVRf— Will Lehman | WillforUAWpresident.org (@WillforUAWpres) February 13, 2026

The WSWS has acknowledged Fain’s links to socialism, reporting that Fain’s former chief of staff, Chris Brooks, and a current union official Jonah Furman, are both Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) members. Furman also previously served as the former communications director for the UAW and was brought on board as Fain’s top assistant after Fain ascended to the union’s presidency, according to Sage Journals.

Furman previously worked for the 2020 presidential campaign of socialist Independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders as well as the congressional campaign of Democratic New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, according to Sage Journals. Brooks left UAW leadership in 2023 after a federal monitor reported him to be involved in improperly attempting to have the duties of the UAW’s secretary-treasurer removed, Reuters reported. He is now a columnist at Jacobin, a socialist magazine.

WSWS condemned the DSA in 2017, saying that it has “anti-socialist politics.” According to the Socialist outlet, the DSA “is a pro-capitalist organization steeped in a tradition of anti-communism and bitterly opposed to the political independence of the working class.”

The DSA represents a wider cast of socialists, claiming that its members are “building progressive movements for social change while establishing an openly democratic socialist presence in American communities and politics,” according to the DSA website.

The WSWS also denounced the UAWD claiming in May 2025, days after at voted to dissolve, that it “was built to block rebellion” and has now “collapsed in on itself.”

Lehman is campaigning to “mobilize the rank and file” to “abolish the corrupt UAW bureaucracy” and “put all power in the hands of workers,” according to his February X post announcing his 2026 presidential bid against Fain.

“Class struggle, not class collaboration!” his post at the time added.

Lehman’s campaign website states that the UAW is “in crisis” under Fain’s leadership, mentioning that more than 5,000 workers have been laid off during Fain’s presidency “while bureaucrats kept their salaries.” He further added that 470 of these UAW “bureaucrats” are paid salaries in the six figures, while Fain himself makes $276,000 annually.

The upstart socialist previously ran in the contentious 2022–23 United Auto Workers international union election in which he finished in a distant fifth place out of five candidates, winning only 4.6% of the vote. Incumbent president Ray Curry and Fain came in first and second place, respectively. Fain narrowly unseated Curry in the runoff.

As it happened, Lehman called the election a “sham” and noted its low turnout saying, “You have 10% of the members participating,” The Detroit News reported at the time.

A paid UAW organizer who publicly supports Fain posted an AI-generated image to Facebook showing a bound and gagged Lehman with a rifle pointed as his head, the Detroit Free Press reported. The Fain supporter received a two-year suspension after posting the image, which WSWS said amounted to a death threat.

“The International Workers Alliance of Rank-and-File Committees (IWA-RFC) calls on workers and all defenders of democratic rights to denounce this incitement to violence against Will Lehman and demand its unequivocal public repudiation by the UAW,” a July 20 WSWS article stated regarding the post.

A top UAW official and Fain supporter posted a death threat against me: an AI-generated image of me bound and gagged at gunpoint. He is paid $202,000 a year from members’ dues. I will not be intimidated, and this campaign will not be stopped. Read my full statement:…— Will Lehman | WillforUAWpresident.org (@WillforUAWpres) July 20, 2026

Lehman is not considered a major threat to unseating Fain in the ongoing 2026 election, as the embattled incumbent union boss faces challenges from Tricia Geiger — who has the endorsement of three former UAW presidents including Curry — and Vice President Rich Boyer. However, Lehman’s support among the leftist grassroots could complicate Fain’s path to another term as support from socialist adjacent groups such as the UAWD were integral to his insurgent 2023 win.

The UAWD was founded in 2019 by members of the DSA, Labor Notes — a “media and organizing project” founded by socialist labor activists — and other advocates claiming to want to reform the UAW amid leadership corruption revealed by a UAW court-appointed monitor, WSWS reported. 

The UAWD, before its 2025 dissolution, was supported by the DSA in its reform efforts, according to a 2020 statement from the prominent socialist group. The DSA encouraged members to support the UAWD in 2021, calling it an “emerging movement inside” the UAW, in a newsletter. This DSA newsletter, which has the tagline “We must struggle together,” urges members to donate to the UAWD, claiming it is “exciting to see rank and file members organizing to take back power in this important industrial union.”

The Rank-and-File Strategy approach of the DSA — which is currently live online and branded with the DSA logo — offers “[a] Game Plan for DSAers” in which it encourages members to “[s]upport union reform caucuses.” It lists the UAWD as one of the two such caucuses it highlights. 

The WSWS is run by the International Committee of the Fourth International (ICFI), which states its goal is “to put an end to the capitalist system and establish socialism on a world scale.”

At the dissolution of the UAWD, the chair and other leaders began “a new, union-wide network to carry on the work of transforming” the UAW called UAW Member Action, the UAWD website notes. The UAW Member Action website claims that Fain has been “steering our union back into the fight,” and includes him as its endorsed presidential candidate for the 2026 UAW election.

UAW Member Action did not respond to the DNCF’s request to elaborate their stance toward socialism and the DSA.

Honored to have the support of UAW president, champion for workers, Shawn Fain. pic.twitter.com/uIrQ12kKhD— Dr. Abdul El-Sayed (@AbdulElSayed) July 3, 2026

Fain and his UAW endorsed now-Democratic Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed during his contentious primary campaign. While a self-professed capitalist, El-Sayed was the furthest left candidate in the race’s Democratic primary field and received endorsements from several prominent socialist figures.

The union boss also, during a Facebook Live in 2023, notably wore a t-shirt bearing the words “Eat The Rich.” The phrase has its origins in the French Revolution and is now often used as an anti-capitalist slogan.

The UAW has more than 400,000 active members and more than 580,000 retired members in the U.S., Canada, and Puerto Rico, the union’s website reports.

Fain traveled around Michigan, the automotive capital of the U.S. where UAW is headquartered, with Sanders to rally for Kamala Harris in 2024, according to multiple X posts from Sanders.

Fain entered UAW leadership with the promise to help the rank and file members of the union; his platform boasted “No corruption. No concessions. No tiers.” In his first year as union president, he led the UAW in a major strike against the Detroit “Big 3” automakers, wherein he fought for cost of living adjustments, ending tiers, and job security, the UAW website claims.

WSWS emphasized how Lehman separated himself from the rest of the candidates, including Fain, by claiming that the UAW’s 2023 strike against the “Big 3” automakers was not a “victory,” as the other candidates claimed.

“It was not a real strike. It was a disaster. It was a Hollywood strike,” he said, according to WSWS.

Arianna Hooker and Senior Investigative Reporter Emily Kopp contributed to this report.

news.title: AOC Admits 'Woke 1 Was Crazy' in Bid to Reframe Democratic Socialism
news.text: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is attempting something few politicians manage to pull off cleanly: convincing the public to forget, or at least forgive, a chapter of left wing politics that many liberals once embraced but now find hard to defend. As the most recognizable face of democratic socialism in the country, Ocasio-Cortez appears to be asking for a second chance on behalf of candidates who once supported ideas like defunding the police. Her argument is that candidates should be evaluated based on where they stand today, not on positions they held years ago. That pitch, however, could be a hard sell for moderate Democrats and Republicans alike, particularly in swing districts far from safely blue territory. What She Actually SaidThe comments came during an appearance on ABC's "This Week" over the weekend, when Ocasio-Cortez was pressed about some of the stances democratic socialists took back around 2020. She described those positions as a reflection of the moment. Laughing as she quoted a fellow politician and friend, she said "Woke 1 was crazy." She went on to say that judging a candidate today means looking closely at what they're actually saying now. While she acknowledged that policy debates in the early days of the pandemic were productive given how dire the situation was at the time, she admitted the language used back then isn't language politicians would reach for today. A Familiar Playbook, With Mixed ResultsOcasio-Cortez isn't the first to try distancing herself from that era. Kamala Harris attempted something similar and it didn't go smoothly. During her brief run for president in 2020, Harris backed several progressive positions, including taxpayer funded gender transition surgeries for federal inmates, decriminalizing border crossings, and banning plastic straws. Four years later, when she stepped in to replace President Biden atop the ticket, Harris tried to rebrand herself as a more centrist, traditional Democrat. The Trump campaign, however, made sure her earlier positions stayed in the spotlight throughout the race. Not Everyone Buys the "Hindsight" ExcuseThere's a catch to framing 2020 era leftist politics as something that only looks bad in hindsight. Plenty of Democrats were raising red flags about it in real time, long before it became politically convenient to do so. Chief among them was Joe Biden himself, who ultimately won both the Democratic primary and the general election running on a center left platform. The Bottom LineOcasio-Cortez's comments seem to be part of a broader effort to reshape what democratic socialism represents, steering it away from social and cultural positions that have become difficult to defend and toward a more populist economic message with wider appeal. Whether that repositioning actually works may become clear depending on what she does next politically, whether that's a run for Senate or a potential presidential bid in 2028.
news.summary: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is striving to reshape perceptions of democratic socialism by urging voters to judge candidates based on their current positions rather than past stances, particularly those related to controversial topics like defunding the police. Her recent comments reflect a desire to distance herself and fellow politicians from earlier leftist politics that have faced backlash.

news.title: Trump sued over plan to sell access to Truth Social posts
news.text:
NEW YORK – Two US media groups on Aug 12 sued President Donald Trump over his move to charge for early access to his often market-moving Truth Social posts.

The lawsuit, filed in New York by The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation, states that the scheme is “extraordinary, corrupt and unconstitutional.”

Subscribers to the paid service are supposed to get almost instantaneous access to Trump’s messages on the Truth Social platform – crucial seconds ahead of the general public.

The billionaire Republican often uses the platform to announce huge news, ranging from developments in the Iran war to trade tariffs, all of which can instantly send market values tumbling or soaring.

Early access to the service can cost up to US$100,000 (S$128,016) per month, or US$60,000 per month if users commit to three years, according to the Aug 12 lawsuit.

“This scheme is profoundly corrupt. The President stands to gain financially by giving ‘market-moving’ government information to those who are willing and able to pay his personal company,” a court filing says.

Trump Media & Technology Group, the company running the platform, has dismissed concerns over the product, which is called Truth API and was first unveiled in mid-July.

Calls for probe

The Intercept, a nonprofit US news outlet, and Freedom of the Press Foundation, which operates a database tracking Truth Social posts, argue that the paid service hinders their ability to properly cover Trump.

“Timely access to the President’s posts is critical for both groups,” the filing states, asking the court to declare Truth API as unlawful and block future posts.

Several Democratic lawmakers have called for a probe into the service by the Securities and Exchange Commission, which regulates US markets.

Trump Media interim CEO Kevin McGurn said this week that Truth API is already generating revenue with 10 customer agreements signed, though he did not identify the clients.

The Wall Street Journal has reported that trading companies were among the first to subscribe to the service.

On Aug 10, Trump Media posted a ten-fold jump in losses for the second quarter of 2026, linked to declines in values of its digital assets.

Trump, like his close relatives, is alleged to have made billions of dollars in his second White House term through cryptocurrency ventures, property deals, stock trades and payouts from lawsuits.

Forbes, a financial media outlet, has estimated that Trump’s net worth shot up from US$2.3 billion to US$6.5 billion since 2024, when he won the election over Kamala Harris. AFP

news.title: This GOP Rep Told His Democratic Opponent To Sue. You’ll Never Guess What Happened Next.
news.text:
After Democrat Bob Harvie sent cease-and-desist letters demanding Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) and his campaign affiliates stop saying Harvie is “under FBI investigation,” Fitzpatrick boasted to HuffPost that his challenger would never follow through with lawsuit threats. 

“They said they were going to file a lawsuit. And guess what? Guess what? They didn’t file a lawsuit,” Fitzpatrick said in an interview last month. He knew his allegation was true, he said, because he’s a former FBI agent and is “well aware of what’s contained in the files that he refuses to release.” A super PAC supporting Fitzpatrick in his reelection campaign in the 1st Congressional District even offered to pay for the lawsuit. 

Last week, Harvie actually sued. He filed a defamation case against Defending America PAC and Chris Pack, a Republican consultant, accusing them of “repeatedly and recklessly publishing false and defamatory statements imputing criminal conduct that go beyond the bounds even of a highly contested political campaign.”

“Put your money where your mouth is,” Harvie said in a statement. “Just tell us where to send the bills. See you in court.”

Fitzpatrick’s campaign officials did not respond to a request for comment, but the lawsuit hasn’t cowed them. Echoing Fitzpatrick, the super PAC put up a new website this week demanding Harvie release his “complete, unredacted FBI grand jury transcript, FD-302 interview reports, grand jury subpoenas, and any and all DOJ correspondence related to the FBI corruption investigation.”

Harvie, a member of the Bucks County Board of Commissioners, testified before a grand jury in 2021 as part of an FBI investigation that never resulted in charges against Harvie or anyone else. Fitzpatrick insists it’s an active case and that only Harvie can prove him wrong by releasing documents showing investigators weren’t probing his conduct. 

Michael Levy, an adjunct professor at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School who worked as an assistant U.S. attorney in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania for 37 years, said grand jury witnesses are not given a stack of records to take with them after they testify and that lots of witnesses are called simply to provide factual information. 

“Federal grand jury proceedings are secret,” Levy told HuffPost. “Nothing should get published unless the grand jury charges somebody. So there’s no effort to identify witnesses, and sometimes there are efforts to make sure that nobody knows they actually came and testified.”

In a July interview with HuffPost, Harvie said he’s got no documents and that Fitzpatrick, a moderate Republican representing a tossup district in a tough election year, was just desperate to keep his job. 

Harvie also took a shot of his own, describing Fitzpatrick as owning multiple fancy homes and being “married to a Fox News reporter who’s considerably younger than he is, and so I just think he’s got a lifestyle he likes now, and he’s desperate.” (Fitzpatrick got married earlier this year.) 

In response, Defending America PAC, the group supporting Fitzpatrick, added the page to its “Fire Bob Harvie” website offering to pay for his lawsuit — and slamming Harvie for “pitching bullshit cease-and-desist stories where Harvie invokes Brian Fitzpatrick’s recent marriage like the scumbag that Harvie is.”

The site went on to say “Harvie’s bank account may be a little tight after his recent divorce” and that “it may have had something to do with Harvie getting a little too cozy with a county employee.” It linked to an image of a Facebook page saying Harvie “banged” a county employee.

“Harvie never cheated on his wife and never had sex with a Bucks County employee,” Harvie’s defamation suit says. “The Facebook Publication directly accuses Harvie of engaging in an extramarital relationship with a Bucks County employee while serving as a Bucks County Commissioner and misusing his public office, in order to destroy his reputation.”

Harvie’s campaign filed its complaint this week against Defending America PAC and Pack, but not the Fitzpatrick campaign itself. A spokesperson for Defending America PAC couldn’t be reached. Pack did not respond to a request for comment through his PR firm. 

Harvie’s campaign sent cease-and-desist letters to the campaign and the super PAC, but not Fitzpatrick’s campaign. A TV ad paid for by Fitzpatrick’s campaign says Harvie is “under FBI investigation” without mentioning the allegation about the county employee.

The nastiness of the campaign may speak to the stakes of the election. Fitzpatrick is one of only three House Republicans representing a district won by Kamala Harris in 2024, and Democrats view it as a prime pickup opportunity.

news.title: Seventy-One Per Cent of Catholics Say Trump Is 'Not Too' or 'Not at All' Religious in New Poll
news.text: Seventy-one per cent of American Catholics now view President Donald Trump as 'not too' or 'not at all' religious, according to comprehensive new polling data from the Pew Research Centre.'Just 5 per cent describe him as very religious, while 80 per cent of Hispanic Catholics say he is not particularly religious,' said the research.The finding underscores a widening perceptual gap among voters who helped fuel his 2024 electoral victory by casting 55 per cent of their ballots in his favour.While conservative Catholics have historically prioritised judicial appointments, religious liberty, and anti-abortion policies over personal piety, the latest metrics indicate a deepening scepticism regarding the president's personal spiritual alignment.This sentiment varies significantly across racial and ethnic lines within the Church, registering most acutely among Hispanic Catholics, who describe the president as lacking traditional religious devotion.Trump's 2024 victory among Catholics was one of the election's biggest religious shifts as Catholics had split almost evenly between Trump and Joe Biden in 2020, but Pew Research found Trump winning 55 per cent of the Catholic vote in 2024, compared with 43 per cent for Kamala Harris.Less than two years into Trump's second term, signs of strain are emerging. Pew found his approval among white Catholics falling from 59 per cent in February 2025 to 52 per cent in January 2026, while approval among Hispanic Catholics dropped from 31 per cent to 23 per cent.For Republicans, the numbers matter ahead of November's midterm elections. But they do not necessarily mean Catholics are abandoning Trump. Instead, they suggest a coalition built around different priorities could become vulnerable when those priorities clash.The Catholic Vote Is Not One VoteThere is no single Catholic vote. American Catholicism includes conservative white voters, Latino Catholics, working-class voters and progressives with very different political priorities.Trump brought enough of those groups together in 2024 to improve on his 2020 performance. Pew found that 7 per cent of Catholics who backed Biden in 2020 switched to Trump, while only 4 per cent of Trump's 2020 Catholic voters moved to Harris. The question now is whether that coalition was durable or transactional.Immigration Exposes a Fault LineImmigration is one area where the coalition could come under pressure. Many Catholics supported tighter border controls, but the Catholic Church's emphasis on the dignity of migrants creates tension with aggressive deportation policies.That tension is particularly important for Hispanic Catholics. Immigration policy is not an abstract issue when those facing deportation may be relatives, parishioners or neighbours.Trump does not necessarily need to lose these voters outright for Republicans to suffer. A voter who remains culturally conservative but becomes less enthusiastic about the president could simply stay home.Abortion Still Pulls Catholics RightAbortion remains an important Republican anchor, although Catholics themselves are divided. Pew found in 2025 that 59 per cent of Catholics believed abortion should be legal in all or most cases, while roughly four-in-ten said it should be illegal in most or all cases.The finding about Trump's religiosity should therefore not be treated as a direct measure of his political support.A Catholic voter can regard Trump as insufficiently religious while still supporting him because of abortion, judicial appointments, religious liberty or cultural issues. Trump does not have to be seen as a religious role model to remain politically useful to conservative Catholics.Pope Leo Creates Another Fault LineTrump also faces an unusual complication in Catholic politics: Pope Leo XIV. About 78 per cent of US Catholics have a favourable view of the American-born pope, according to Pew. More than half, 51 per cent, said Trump had been too critical of Leo.That gives Catholic voters a religious authority whose disagreements with Trump can carry political weight. Leo and Trump have clashed over issues, including migrants and foreign policy. The divide is not absolute, but the tension gives disaffected Catholics another way to view the president.Why Evangelicals Are DifferentTrump's relationship with white evangelicals has also cooled, but the group remains firmly aligned with him. Pew found approval among white evangelical Protestants falling from 78 per cent in February 2025 to 69 per cent in January 2026.Even after that decline, evangelicals remained one of Trump's strongest religious constituencies.Their support has become closely tied to cultural and political identity. Many voters view Trump less as a religious role model than as a political defender of conservative Christianity.Catholics are less politically cohesive. Their support can therefore be more sensitive to individual issues, particularly immigration and Trump's relationship with the pope.Midterm Turnout Is The Real RiskRepublicans do not need Catholics to become Democrats for declining support to matter. A relatively small number of 2024 Trump voters staying home or splitting their ticket could prove consequential in closely contested races.The risk may be greatest among Hispanic Catholics, where Trump's approval is already considerably lower than among white Catholics.None of this means Catholics are about to abandon Trump or the Republican Party. His coalition retains powerful support on abortion, religious liberty and cultural issues.But the latest polling exposes an important distinction. Trump's evangelical base is deeply embedded in cultural identity, while Catholic support is more fragmented and issue-driven. That made Catholics one of the keys to Trump's 2024 victory. It could also make them one of the groups Republicans cannot afford to take for granted in November.Ultimately, the revelation that a substantial majority of Catholics view Trump as minimally religious does not signal an immediate mass exodus from the party. Instead, it serves as an indicator that the transactional alignment between religious voters and the administration remains subject to continuous cost-benefit evaluations on the ground.

news.title: Trump sued over sale of access to Truth Social posts
news.text:
Two US media groups on Wednesday sued President Donald Trump over his move to charge for early access to his often market-moving Truth Social posts.

The lawsuit, filed in New York by The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation, states that the scheme is “extraordinary, corrupt and unconstitutional.”

Subscribers to the paid service are supposed to get almost instantaneous access to Trump’s messages on the Truth Social platform — crucial seconds ahead of the general public.

The billionaire Republican often uses the platform to announce huge news, ranging from developments in the Iran war to trade tariffs.

Early access to the service can cost up to $100,000 per month, or $60,000 per month if users commit to three years, according to Wednesday’s lawsuit.

“This scheme is profoundly corrupt. The President stands to gain financially by giving ‘market-moving’ government information to those who are willing and able to pay his personal company,” a court filing says.

Trump Media & Technology Group, the company running the platform, has dismissed concerns over the product, which is called Truth API and was first unveiled in mid-July.

– Calls for probe –

The Intercept, a nonprofit US news outlet, and Freedom of the Press Foundation, which operates a database tracking Truth Social posts, argue that the paid service hinders their ability to properly cover Trump.

“Timely access to the president’s posts is critical for both groups,” the filing states, asking the court to declare Truth API as unlawful and block future posts.

Several Democratic lawmakers have called for a probe into the service by the Securities and Exchange Commission, which regulates US markets.

Trump Media interim Chief Executive Officer, Kevin McGurn, said this week that Truth API is already generating revenue with 10 customer agreements signed, though he did not identify the clients.

The Wall Street Journal has reported that trading companies were among the first to subscribe to the service.

On Monday, Trump Media posted a ten-fold jump in losses for the second quarter of 2026, linked to declines in values of its digital assets.

Forbes, a financial media outlet, has estimated that Trump’s net worth shot up from $2.3 billion to $6.5 billion since 2024, when he won the election over Kamala Harris.
