news.title: Bruce Blakeman Surges in Race to Defeat Hochul and Flip New York—New Poll
news.text: Republican Bruce Blakeman is gaining ground on Democratic Governor Kathy Hochul in the New York governor race, according to a new poll released by Siena University on Wednesday. New York has long been viewed as one of the most Democratic states in the country, but recent cycles have seen Democrats’ margins shrink in the state. Former Vice President Kamala Harris won the Empire State by fewer than 13 points, down from former President Joe Biden’s 23-point victory in 2020. Hochul herself had a closer-than-expected election in 2022, defeating then-Representative Lee Zeldin by only about 6 points. Hochul’s relatively poor showing four years ago, as well as recent trends, have fueled Republicans’ hopes of making the governor race competitive this year. Republicans will also work to tie Hochul and other moderate Democrats to the more progressive lawmakers elected in New York City’s primaries, many of whom identify as democratic socialists. But Democrats have noted that Hochul is more well-known and popular compared to her last election, and that the national environment looks to be better for Democrats due to President Donald Trump’s declining national approval rating, the unpopular Iran war, and growing concerns about the economy and cost-of-living. Hochul’s Lead Shrinks In New York Governor Poll Hochul held a 10-point lead over Blakeman, the current Nassau County executive, in the new poll, which surveyed 811 likely voters from August 3-6, 2026. Hochul’s support stood at 49 percent, compared to Blakeman’s 39 percent. That marks a tightening race from their June poll, when Hochul had a 20-point lead, 52 percent to 32 percent. Hochul led by 16 points, 49 percent to 33 percent, in April; and 13 points, 47 percent to 34 percent, in March. Blakeman’s 39 percent support is his highest vote share in a Siena poll. The new poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.2 percentage points for the sample who answered the core questions. Other Democrats performed better than Hochul in the poll. In the attorney general race, Democrat Letitia James held an 18-point lead over Republican Saritha Komatireddy, 54 percent to 36 percent. State Comptroller Tom DiNapoli held a 32-point lead over Republican Joseph Hernandez. Boris Heersink, professor of political science at Fordham University, told Newsweek it is “a little surprising to see Hochul do worse in this poll than the other Democratic candidates.” “But overall, a ten point lead is still a very comfortable one and Hochul is doing better in this poll than she did in the 2022 race. It seems extremely unlikely that Hochul will lose in November; the electorate in the state is still comfortably majority Democrat,” he said. Joseph Viteritti, the Thomas Hunter Professor of Public Policy at Hunter College, told Newsweek Hochul still has a “safe lead” but it’s not surprising that Blakeman is “picking up momentum as he gains wider recognition among potential voters.” Blakeman responded to the poll in a statement to Newsweek. “All of the polls we have seen in the last two months have us virtually tied with Kathy Hochul. This poll is always off and continues to be off. We know and she knows this race is neck and neck. Kathy Hochul is desperate for people to believe that she is way ahead when she knows that her high taxes, soaring electric bills, and increased crime have made her the worst governor in America,” Blakeman said. Newsweek also reached out to Hochul’s campaign for comment via email. What Do Other Polls and Forecasts Show? A co/efficient poll, which surveyed 1,085 likely voters from June 30-July 2, 2026, showed Hochul up 6 points, 47 percent to 41 percent, with 12 percent saying they were undecided about who they would support. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points and was first reported by The New York Post. An Echelon Insights poll, conducted among 500 registered voters from March 24-26, 2026, showed Hochul up 15 points, 55 percent to 40 percent. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 5.4 percentage points and was first reported by Politico. The race is considered to be safe and solid Democratic by forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball. Hochul is also favored in prediction markets. Her chances of victory stood at 94 percent on both Kalshi and Polymarket as of Wednesday morning. Prediction markets allow traders to buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real‑money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always accurately predict the future. Some Democrats believed Hochul would be vulnerable in a Democratic primary, and her Lieutenant Governor Antonio Delgado sought to launch a primary against her. However, he ultimately dropped out of the primary, allowing Hochul to win renomination. Hochul also received the endorsement of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. “New Yorkers deserve leaders who believe in transformation. Leaders who understand that hope is inspired by a vision, and sustained by change. Governor Kathy Hochul has earned my endorsement because she has chosen to govern in that spirit. And in this moment, that choice matters,” Mamdani wrote in an opinion article for The Nation. Viteritti said her solid relationship with Mamdani could prevent left-wing defections. “Hochul and Mamdani understand that they need each other to govern, especially with the budget challenges ahead of them,” he said. Progressives Surge in NYC—Could That Hurt Democrats Statewide? The New York Democratic primaries were defined by progressive victories. Darializa Avila-Chevalier, a democratic socialist, and Brad Lander, the former New York City comptroller, defeated more moderate Democratic incumbents, while state Representative Claire Valdez, a democratic socialist, also won an open congressional seat. Other democratic socialists and progressives also won in local races. Republicans are hoping the rise in more progressive Democrats could alienate more moderate swing voters and give them an opening to win back support in November. They are hoping to tie Hochul, who is viewed as a fairly mainstream Democrat, to those candidates. Blakeman told The New York Post on Tuesday that Hochul is “doing everything that Zohran Mamdani wants her to do” because “he’s running the party now.” Heersink said he is doubtful that these progressive victories will damage Democrats statewide. “The midterm elections are likely to be mostly centered on voters turning out for or against the Trump administration. In gubernatorial races there is more space to show disagreements with the parties and their candidates since it doesn't involve Congressional majorities. But most voters will be relatively consistent in what parties they vote for,” he said. Is New York Becoming a Purple State? Democratic margins have shrunk in New York, and it had one of the largest rightward shifts from 2020 to 2024. Republicans made gains in New York City’s outer boroughs among Latino and Asian voters, and crime has been viewed as a major force behind Democrats’ slipping margins. This year’s elections could help gauge whether Republicans will continue to make inroads with voters in the state or whether Democratic support could rebound. Democrats still have a massive lead in terms of voter registration in New York. There were 6,445,605 registered Democrats and 2,994,839 registered Republicans statewide as of February 20, according to the New York State Board of Elections. New York has not elected a Republican governor since George Pataki’s reelection in 2002. Contact Newsweek editor on this story: Edward Pearcey.
news.summary: New York Governor Kathy Hochul's lead shrunk in a new poll of the Empire State released on Wednesday.

Is a new, underwater front opening in the data center wars? Maine Public profiles a new proposal to build a “submerged” data center in Passamaquoddy Bay. The idea was famously tested in Microsoft’s Project Natick off the coast of Scotland in a pilot program that hasn’t been active in years; Maine Public notes that “earlier this year, another submerged data center was reportedly deployed in China.” Residents of Eastport, Maine, who worry about damage to the local economy, particularly if the data center heat drives out the lobsters, are having none of it. “Speakers from across the political spectrum lambasted the idea” at a recent gathering, Maine Public reports. One of the more memorable quotes, from Eastport City Manager Brian Schuth: “I have said it’s the equivalent of an idea scrawled on a bar napkin.” Of note: Both chambers of Maine’s state legislature passed a temporary moratorium on data centers larger than 20 megawatts this past spring—a measure spearheaded by state Democrats—only for Democratic Governor Janet Mills to veto. The measure would not have affected Passamaquoddy Bay, though, as the application by developer DeepGreen Western Passage would not meet this threshold. —Heather Souvaine Horn

The Ideas Factory

Resources for the Future publishes a new working paper from Yanjun “Penny” Liao, Hannah Druckenmiller, and Margaret A. Walls on the urgent topic of how weather extremes are affecting the federal crop insurance program, or FCIP. news.title: What Is Usha Vance Thinking?
news.text:
JD Vance posted on X an announcement signed by both him and his wife. Usha reshared his post. Neither posted a photo. But Donald Trump did, early the following day, on Truth Social: The Vances’ son Vivek held the baby while his sister, Mirabel, looked on. The president and vice president claimed the moment; Usha receded into the background.
She knows the drill by now. In Trump’s Washington, even your child’s first photo op runs through the boss.
On April 23, about three months before Alec’s birth, Usha introduced Melania Trump at the 113th annual First Lady’s Luncheon, calling her a “woman of many accomplishments…and my friend.” When Melania walked to the podium, she barely acknowledged Usha, aside from giving a perfunctory “thank you” after the second lady turned the page of Melania’s speech. Usha stood by, beaming, her expression inscrutable.
It’s a posture she has perfected: present, useful, and almost invisible. If she is at all disturbed by the nativist Republican Party her husband has come to represent, she never shows it, at least not publicly. Like many ambitious spouses of powerful politicians, Usha has learned to operate in private—a quiet architect content to let her husband stand in the light while she does the load-bearing work off camera.
Make no mistake: Usha Vance, like Melania Trump, is not a woman to be pitied. She has helped to build, carefully and mostly out of view, the JD Vance we know today. When I ask a friend of the Vances from Yale Law School whether they think Usha disapproves of her husband’s right-wing populism and social conservatism, they scoff. “It’s patronizing to say that she’s been silenced,” they say. “She has chosen this.”
“She built JD into this creation of the coastal Acela corridor. It’s not an immigrant story; it’s a meritocracy story,” another Yale Law classmate tells me, speaking on condition of anonymity for fear of retribution. “She radiates authority and a sense of purpose and mission.” Usha, says the Yale Law friend, “saw tremendous potential in JD.” Those in their Yale Law cohort have been so stunned by the Vances’ rapid ascent to the highest echelon of American politics—and their about-face on Trump and the MAGA movement—that they’ve created a Signal group where they feel they can safely compare notes. (Assuming nobody accidentally invites Jeffrey Goldberg to join the chat.)
Usha Chilukuri was born in 1986 to Indian Hindu immigrants and grew up in an upper-middle-class San Diego suburb with her younger sister, Shreya. The Vances often post photos of their children, but Usha’s parents and sister don’t appear in her social media feeds. They are very private people and very well educated. Usha’s sister graduated from Duke University in 2012 with a Bachelor of Science in engineering. Her father, Radhakrishna “Krish” Chilukuri, is a retired aerospace engineer who now lectures in the Department of Aerospace Engineering at San Diego State University. Her mother, Lakshmi, is a molecular biologist who serves as a provost at UC San Diego. She helped establish a pilot course on race, ethnicity, and gender in biology and medicine; has written about the university’s commitment to diversity; and once served on the school’s biological sciences diversity committee—her son-in-law, however, has made dismantling DEI and deriding “wokeness” a centerpiece of his political career.
When asked about the contradiction in 2025, as CBS News reported on his mother-in-law’s academic work, the vice president offered a version of a family détente: “I don’t like DEI, and I’m proud of what our administration has done on that front,” he said. “But I love my mother-in-law. If she doesn’t share my views on DEI, I suppose I’ll have to do what 99% of Americans do when confronted with a family member who doesn’t always agree with them: get over it.”
Usha, who declined an interview for this story, was comfortable operating in the exclusive world of elite academic institutions well before she met her husband—and it seems she has always enjoyed a challenge. In 2006, when she was a junior at Yale—nearly two decades before she became second lady in a Republican administration—the irreverent (and more than a little dated) campus tabloid Rumpus featured her as one of the college’s “50 most beautiful” students. A photo caption described her smile as being “as bright as the San Diego sun,” while an article deemed her politics to be “of the leftish political persuasion.” Her taste in men, the item noted, ran in the other direction: “She does like a man who has a lot to say for himself. In the past, most of her liaisons have been tall, handsome, and conservative.”
She graduated summa cum laude from Yale in 2007 with a degree in history, then earned a master’s degree from Cambridge before enrolling at Yale Law. Usha and JD met in 2010 during their first year of law school. The vice president later recalled his first impression of his future wife, characterizing her as “a combination of every positive quality a human being should have: bright, hardworking, tall, and beautiful.” They became friends immediately, but it wasn’t until their second semester—when he began opening up to her about being raised by his grandparents in a working-class town in Ohio and having a strained relationship with his mother, who struggled with addiction—that he won her over. Usha told Meghan McCain in an interview last year that she came to think of him as one of “the more interesting people I’d ever met in my life.” By their third year, they were living together with their beloved German shepherd, Casper.
Usha’s political views were, even then, difficult to read. Classmates tell me she rarely gossiped and seldom voiced strong opinions. “It was never about anything other than achievement,” one says. “She was the quintessential, ubiquitous Yale Law student whom I like to call a ‘gold star chaser.’ Usha took it to the next level. I never understood why she was trying so hard.” The couple had celebrity status on campus and earned their own nickname: Judusha, a mash-up of JD, Usha, and “judicial.”
Usha became something like JD’s spirit guide to elite institutional life, coaching him on the unspoken rules he hadn’t grown up with. In his best-selling 2016 memoir, Hillbilly Elegy, JD recalls her teaching him which utensils to use at a formal dinner—go from the outside in—and according to friends, she once kept a spreadsheet of things she thought he should try, like Greek yogurt. Just as he made a career of translating the white working class for coastal elites, she introduced him to the customs of the top 5 percent.
The Vances, per The New York Times, had a civil wedding in Kentucky in 2014 and then a separate Hindu ceremony. Both went on to build the kind of résumé their Yale classmates would covet for themselves. Usha clerked for a series of Republican-appointed judges, including US District Court judge Amul Thapar in eastern Kentucky and Judge Brett Kavanaugh on the US Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit.
Her affection for Kavanaugh would later resurface as one explanation for the broader rightward drift in her own politics. Usha was reportedly appalled by how the future Supreme Court justice was treated during his contentious 2018 confirmation hearings, after psychology professor Christine Blasey Ford accused him of sexually assaulting her decades earlier, which he denied. That isn’t to say that Usha always agreed with her husband’s politics: A friend, according to The Washington Post, said she was disturbed by Trump’s incitement of the January 6 riot. (The second lady’s office did not respond to a request for comment.) A year later, her husband sharply criticized the congressional investigation into the insurrection. JD, who was running for Senate at the time, went so far as to say that the probe was creating an environment that would make “Americans enemies of the state in their own country.”
JD has since defended Trump’s conduct in the run-up to and during the Capitol attack; criticized his predecessor Mike Pence for how he handled certifying the 2020 election results; and, in an interview with CNN’s Kaitlan Collins, cast doubt on whether Pence’s life was ever truly in danger that day.
Through it all, she’s been described by friends and her own husband as a moderating force. “Even at my best,” JD writes in Hillbilly Elegy, “I’m a delayed explosion—I can be defused, but only with skill and precision. It’s not just that I’ve learned to control myself, but that Usha has learned how to manage me.” Ken Blackwell, Ohio’s secretary of state from 1999 to 2007 and a current senior fellow at the conservative Christian Family Research Council, has visited the Vances at their home in Cincinnati and describes the couple as having “distinctly different carriages of their personhood. Usha comes from a family that pays attention to small things and detail. JD is, at times, a bigger-picture guy and is likely to have a higher risk orientation than Usha, but they balance each other out well.” He adds: “She has a quiet confidence that exhibits itself in understated ways. When she’s made a decision, you come away knowing that she’s thought it through.”
Much has been made of JD’s political evolution from Hillbilly Elegy–era media darling and outspoken Never Trumper to one of the president’s most reliable defenders. His original memoir was once embraced by progressives who saw him as a translator for the Rust Belt voters who helped Trump get elected the first time. JD seemed as surprised as anyone by Trump’s 2016 win: In the run-up to that election, he called Trump “reprehensible” and an “idiot,” and told one former roommate he thought Trump could be “America’s Hitler.” Over time, though, JD became one of the president’s most outspoken supporters. In 2022, backed by billionaire Peter Thiel and endorsed by Trump in the Republican primary, he ran for US Senate in Ohio and won. That is when he started making obvious moves to curry Trump’s favor, like questioning the congressional investigation into January 6.
Usha’s own reported change of heart is harder to pin down. A woman shaped by elite, diversity-minded institutions, Usha is not backing MAGA without reservations, but she is firmly in her husband’s corner—and after the president himself, JD is the most visible supporter of the MAGA movement, as well as one of its most vocal adherents. This March, in an NBC News interview promoting her childhood-literacy podcast, Storytime With the Second Lady, Usha told correspondent Kate Snow about working with her husband: “There are conversations all the time…. When something is troubling him, that’s when I come into the picture.” She also acknowledged that she doesn’t always agree with the vice president or the administration’s policies, but she said that no one in her political orbit had ever taken her to task for it.
For a couple that models an easy domestic partnership, it was notable when, on a Father’s Day podcast episode released in June, JD joined Usha as a guest to read Winnie-the-Pooh and greeted his wife on camera with two brisk pats on her knee. The interaction went viral for how stilted it looked, prompting one commentator to crack that there was more visible chemistry during the Iran negotiations. Usha declined to respond to the hubbub, a nonreaction that was itself the point: However she felt about being patted like a child, she let the moment pass without comment.
In a political culture where image is everything, Usha’s unfussy presentation reads as a quiet rejection of the performative style associated with other women around Trump—something that may or may not be intentional, but that lands as a message all the same.
During the campaign, Usha helped prepare her husband for his vice presidential debate and became one of his most effective defenders. When JD faced backlash for a 2021 Tucker Carlson interview in which he said the country was being run by “a bunch of childless cat ladies who are miserable at their own lives,” Usha pushed back on the framing: “I took a moment to look and actually see what he had said and try to understand what the context was,” she said. “Because what he was really saying is that it can be really hard to be a parent in this country. And sometimes our policies are designed in a way that makes it even harder.”
She also endured racist attacks over her Indian heritage. After Trump chose JD as his running mate, white nationalist Nick Fuentes questioned how JD could “support white identity” while having an Indian wife. In an August 2024 interview on ABC News’ This Week, JD responded: “Look, my attitude to these people attacking my wife is, she’s beautiful, she’s smart. What kind of man marries Usha? A very smart man and a very lucky man, importantly…. Don’t attack my wife. She’s out of your league.”
Some 14 years after they’d met as unlikely equals at Yale, “out of your league” landed as more than a talking point.
But this is not a woman who enters into anything blindly. She is, at 40, the youngest second lady since the Truman administration, as well as the first woman of color, the first Indian American, and the first Hindu to hold the role—an office that’s rather thinly defined. (Its acronym, SLOTUS, doesn’t exactly roll off the tongue.) When JD became vice president, they already had three children, all under the age of 10.
The family manages to live a semiprivate life, which is possible in part because of where they live. The vice president’s residence sits on the grounds of the US Naval Observatory, in a leafy pocket of northwest Washington—less than three miles from the White House, but a world away in spirit. “I would always say that people would forget about us because we were a little island away from 1600 [Pennsylvania Avenue]. It was the best of both worlds,” Elizondo says of his years with the Bidens. “They would go to the White House, and they would come home, and they would be able to go sit out on their porch and have a glass of wine and not have people at the gate looking at them. I think the Vances must find that to be very comforting, especially with young kids. There’s plenty of space for extended family.”
Usha tries to lead as normal a life as she can—taking exercise classes, making Costco runs with the kids to stock their lunch boxes, and participating in a book club. She also plays four square and does recess duty at her son’s Catholic school in Bethesda, Maryland, where the Secret Service maintains a presence.
Some parents were worried that the Secret Service would attract attention; having the second family at the school “challenged professionalism and Catholicism,” as one school administrator tells me, “but everyone has risen to the challenge.” Even those who don’t agree politically with the vice president and second lady manage to separate the personal from the political. “Some parents are excited to see the Vances at back-to-school night,” says the administrator. “Others are like, ‘Whatever.’” There has been a sense of relief, they add, that “no one has acted like a fool.”
Most second ladies can live in relative obscurity if they choose to, but the Vances run the risk of causing a scene whenever they venture out. (Kamala Harris won DC by 92.5% in 2024.) Yet Usha’s steady confidence makes it seem as though she is prepared for anything—the product of a mindset she built well before four children entered the picture. One Yale Law classmate, Peter Hamilton, who spoke to The Washington Post, remembered visiting Usha’s room while she was part of a prestigious teaching program in China and finding hundreds of color-coded Post-it notes breaking her days into 15- and 30-minute increments. She has sometimes still run on that system. When Meghan McCain asked last year how she handled raising three young children, Usha said: “When they were little, we tried to think of life in almost like 15-minute blocks—what can we do with Vivek [the middle child] for 15 minutes before he then starts trying to tear apart the furniture? What can we do for the next 15 minutes?”
Regardless of party, the vice president and their spouse usually share an instinct for their place in the political pecking order. The second lady isn’t expected to weigh in on day-to-day affairs, and getting out ahead of one’s skis is a risk no SLOTUS wants to take, especially in a White House where any hint of overshadowing the president—particularly a president singularly focused on dominating every news cycle—is frowned upon.
Usha is adept at seeming uninterested in a future inside the White House. She told McCain that she missed the house the Vances bought in Cincinnati, and when McCain asked about her potentially becoming first lady, Usha demurred: “In a dream world, eventually I’ll be able to live in my home and kind of continue my career and all those sorts of things. And if that happens in four years, I understand. If that happens at some other point in the future, I understand. [I’m] just sort of along for the ride and enjoying it while I can.”
When NBC’s Kate Snow asked Usha last March whether she felt comfortable in MAGA world, Usha tilted her head and answered with a question of her own—“What do you mean?”—without disputing the question’s premise. “No one has ever asked me to engage in any kind of litmus test on anything,” she said. “I don’t feel like I have to walk around pretending anything of any sort. Sometimes I have thoughts that fit very comfortably into one side or another; sometimes I have views that are way more idiosyncratic. It’s a world that I think is actually rather accepting of that, since everyone knows that I really care greatly about JD’s success.” When Snow asked her about MAGA hats, she was similarly unbothered: “I don’t really own any hats. I think I have a Disneyland hat, I want to say. Not a hat lady.”
Anita McBride, who served as chief of staff to first lady Laura Bush, credits Usha with correctly reading the assignment. “It’s not easy to be spouse of the VP—that’s not new. Whether you have kids or not, you don’t want to overstep any boundaries with the White House,” McBride says. By building her public role around childhood literacy, Usha, in McBride’s view, has made a wise decision “to advocate for something that any mother cares about.”
That platform hasn’t shielded her from Washington’s uglier rituals. In February 2025, Trump removed half of The Kennedy Center’s board of trustees, named himself chairman, and replaced those ousted with allies, including Usha. The following month, the Vances were met with about 30 seconds of boos when they took their seats at The Kennedy Center for a National Symphony Orchestra performance. As the onslaught crested, JD waved and smiled; Usha stayed seated beside him, her focus calm and straight ahead. The two remained at the venue for the entire show.
Elizabeth Haenle, who served as social secretary to Vice President Dick Cheney and managed the vice presidential residence, says that Usha is navigating her position—as the first nonwhite second lady in a movement often associated with nativism—through subtlety rather than silence. “She’s got a platform whether she likes it or not,” Haenle says, pointing to the Vances’ visit last year to the Taj Mahal in Agra, India, during a four-day tour. “When she puts her family in front of the Taj Mahal in traditional clothing, that sends a message.”
That hope, and Usha’s role in his religious life more broadly, form a through line in JD’s second memoir, Communion: Finding My Way Back to Faith, published by Harper in June as a follow-up to Hillbilly Elegy. The book traces his 2019 conversion to Catholicism and recounts an April 2025 trip to the Vatican, where the vice president, as he writes, found officials reluctant to say anything substantive about immigration beyond “platitudes” and “clichés” about treating migrants humanely; his audience with Pope Francis, whose health was already failing, came the day before the pope died.
Usha appears throughout the book as both witness and quiet skeptic. JD describes an epiphany he had in a cathedral in Burgundy, France, while vacationing with Usha and their young child. The realization that Catholicism was for him arrived, fittingly, during the brief period when his wife stepped away to use the restroom. Elsewhere, he writes in praise of her: “Usha is so humble and delicate that you don’t realize 99 percent of the time that she is a fierce intellect and extremely tough.” In one passage, after Usha recommends that he read Joan Didion’s The Year of Magical Thinking because she “found it to be cathartic,” JD says goodnight, then looks up the word cathartic in the dictionary and reports the definition back to his readers.
The book is dedicated to Usha, who remains Hindu and has not converted—even as, according to her husband, she is often the one making sure that their children are well-behaved at Sunday Mass. She once told him: “Therapy didn’t work for you, but church does.”
JD has shown a similar reluctance to draw lines when defending his family from his movement’s fringes. At Turning Point USA’s annual convention in December 2025, amid a bitter internal debate over whether the right should platform figures like the antisemitic podcaster Nick Fuentes—the same person who previously attacked Usha over her race—the vice president came down firmly against “purity tests.” “I didn’t bring a list of conservatives to denounce or to deplatform,” he said in his closing speech, adding that the movement should welcome anyone who loves America, “white or black, rich or poor, young or old, rural or urban, controversial or a little bit boring, or somewhere in between.” Erika Kirk, who took over Turning Point after her husband Charlie’s assassination and has floated JD as a possible successor to Trump, endorsed the approach.
One of the Vances’ Yale Law classmates offers a read on the calculation behind the statement. “Usha must have been okay with it. JD is an old-fashioned man who wants to protect his family, and unless she went along with it, he never would have not defended her. He is quick to anger and he’s very loyal. The choice not to criticize Nick Fuentes and people like him in the Republican Party—that is a choice.”
As JD has ascended, Usha has made real sacrifices: giving up a legal career, absorbing racist attacks, and dealing with threats to her family’s safety, including a planned attack against Trump and his top officials during the White House Correspondents’ Dinner on April 25. Whether her personal beliefs fully align with her husband’s, or with those of the party he now represents, may matter less than it once would have. As Ken Blackwell puts it to me, unprompted, in a follow-up call after we’ve spoken about Usha’s history as a registered Democrat: “I was thinking about what you said. You mentioned her being a Democrat. Well…so was Trump!”
Their new arrival is one reason the Vances have been retreating from Washington more than ever. As they settle into life as a family of six, the Vances—similarly to Jack and Jackie Kennedy before them—are renting property in Middleburg, Virginia, roughly 40 miles from Washington. They are leasing part of a sprawling, historic country estate known as Wolver Hill Farm from a firm led by Chuck Kuhn, whose moving company has ushered several presidents into and out of the White House. Their primary home remains their residence at the Naval Observatory, and JD is expected to join his family in Middleburg only occasionally; his attorney has said the vice president will pay fair market rent. The Secret Service has reportedly been assigned to protect the family in Virginia horse country as well.
For now, it seems Usha is still taking life in 15-minute increments—at least until 2027, when her husband, should he choose to run, could begin ramping up a campaign for president. If that day comes, Blackwell expects Usha to follow Barbara Bush’s playbook rather than invent her own. “Barbara Bush wasn’t a movement conservative, but she was a person of great dignity and carriage, and I think that’s the way Usha would be,” he says. Like Usha, Bush was known to keep her own counsel—she was privately pro-choice, but rarely said so in public. Based on the evidence so far, that’s how Usha Vance would likely approach being first lady: She would continue to stand by her man.
news.summary: “It’s patronizing to say that she’s been silenced,” one Yale Law classmate says of JD Vance’s wife, who has perfected the art of knowing where she stands in the Trump administration’s political pecking order. “She has chosen this.”
news.author: Kate Andersen Brower

news.title: Rosie O’Donnell credits Trump for making her ‘re-famous’ as White House calls her ‘obsessed’
news.text:
Rosie O’Donnell credited President Donald Trump for her re-discovered fame on Tuesday as the White House continued to call the actress and former co-host of “The View” “obsessed.”

“I feel like recently I’m re-famous. That’s what I feel. I told my kids, well kids, hold on ’cause mommy’s re-famous. I don’t know how it happened. I think it’s Mango Mussolini,” O’Donnell told “Good Hang” host Amy Poehler, referring to Trump.

“I think it’s him who did it. He didn’t know. If he knew how much he was helping my career and my life, he would shut up about me because, you know, he’s a horrible creature.”

O’Donnell and the president have traded barbs over the years, as the comedian remains one of Trump’s fiercest critics.

She moved to Ireland after Trump’s 2024 election victory over former Vice President Kamala Harris.

The comedian has appeared on multiple podcasts and shows, and she is set to guest host Jimmy Kimmel’s show for a week beginning next week.

The White House pointed Fox News Digital to one of Trump’s Truth Social posts from June 6.

The post shows four images of O’Donnell with Trump appearing in thought bubbles near her head. The caption says O’Donnell “is obsessed.”

O’Donnell recently claimed that she and Trump’s decades-long feud has gone on in part because of their shared roots.

“There have been so many comedians who have said things about him, but I am from the same area that he’s from,” she told Variety in July.

She and Trump were born and raised in New York, and O’Donnell said that people occasionally tell her that they sound alike, “which is probably the worst thing that you can say to me.”

“But I think I’m one of those tough girls from elementary school and junior high that said to him, ‘Shut the hell up! You’re not playing with us. Get out of here, you freakin’ idiot!’ And he never got past it. I think I trigger him like a PTSD response of all his failures in his life as a kid.”

She theorized that she reminds Trump “of the girls who said, ‘You’re nothing,’ and it scares him.”

O’Donnell made similar comments this week on Sophia Bush’s “Work in Progress” podcast. When Bush said that Trump is “obsessed” with her, she agreed and said Trump “grew up with girls like me — tough, probably gay Irish girls who didn’t take s— from no stupid rich boy wannabe.”

O’Donnell also signaled she would be returning to ABC’s “The View” for a 30th anniversary episode in the upcoming season after detailing a tense moment with host and moderator Whoopi Goldberg.

The show’s producer, Brian Teta, posted on X that no official invites for the anniversary had gone out, appearing to refute O’Donnell.

“We love seeing all the excitement about The View’s 30th, lots of plans are in the works, but no invites have gone out,” he wrote.
news.summary: "If he knew how much he was helping my career and my life, he would shut up about me because, you know, he's a horrible creature."
news.author: Fox News

news.title: Who Framed AOC?
news.text: In the mid-1980s, Stanford researchers made 144 students watch 36 minutes of network coverage of the Beirut massacre. Pro-Israel students detected anti-Israel propaganda. Pro-Arab students detected pro-Israel propaganda. The neutral students apparently watched without detecting anything. What a time to be alive. The researchers called it the “hostile media phenomenon,” which, arguably, became the “hostile media business model.” It wasn’t about ignorance. The more knowledgeable people felt, the more bias they perceived. My mind turned to the question of ignorance and whether there is any bliss to be found therein when you, dear readers, assessed a Newsweek article headlined, “AOC’s Chances of Beating Newsom and Harris in New 2028 Michigan Poll.” Fifty-five percent called it fair. Yet 36 percent said it leaned left and 9 percent said it leaned right, making it a rare example of a story where bias to either side approached the fair votes. Weirdly, zero votes came from Michigan. The people whose political judgment the story purported to explain remained silent. Pleading the Fifth—like Anthony Fauci, everyone’s at it nowadays. The timing was perfect. Michigan Democrats later chose AOC-backed Abdul El-Sayed over Haley Stevens after an AIPAC-affiliated group spent more than $30 million intervening in a primary that became an argument about Israel and who speaks for Jewish Democrats. Four decades after the Stanford experiment, Michigan supplied another Israel-flavored political Rorschach test. Perhaps conservative readers saw “AOC” in a headline about a hot-button race and reached for the left-bias button. So, for those readers, here is the right-leaning version. I haven’t had to change a single fact. AOC Trails Buttigieg by Double Digits in New Michigan Poll The progressive congresswoman received 10.7 percent, less than half Pete Buttigieg’s 24.2 percent. She also trailed Jon Ossoff at 13.9 percent, while 21.7 percent were undecided. Her 0.7-point advantage over Gavin Newsom was comfortably inside the four-point margin of error. All true. Also true: AOC beat Newsom and Kamala Harris in the polling. The original article headline simply compared her with the candidates below her rather than those above her. A woman in third place became the protagonist of a story about winning, above a potential candidate—Harris—whom Newsweek once described as illustrating “the insanity theory” of Democratic politics. That does not make the article false, but it makes “but every fact was accurate” a fairly flimsy defense. Facts do not select their own protagonist, comparison or headline. More often, bias hides inside a preposition: AOC was ahead of Newsom; AOC was behind Buttigieg. It was Newsweek that called the angle. The hostile-media phenomenon is real. But it can also become a magnificent escape hatch for journalists: If readers perceive bias, that merely demonstrates how biased the readers are. Heads we’re objective; tails you need therapy. Perhaps the voters crying “left” were partisan cranks, but perhaps they also noticed the frame. The poll put AOC in third place. That’s far from enough for a victory speech.
news.summary: On the Contrary: The same congresswoman is either formidable or finished.
news.author: Christopher Roberts

news.title: Ronald Brownstein: Democrats are about to test the left's big theory
news.text:
Democratic voters are setting up a high-stakes, real-world messaging test in the states most important to their hopes of recapturing the presidency.

The most direct path back to the White House for Democrats in 2028 is to retake Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, the three states that President Donald Trump in 2016 and 2024 dislodged from what I once called "the blue wall."

Last week's Michigan primary advanced candidates who embody the party's competing theories of how best to do so: centrist Jocelyn Benson, the gubernatorial nominee, and Abdul El-Sayed, a Bernie Sanders-style progressive running for Senate. Which one performs better in November will offer the party important clues about which approach can build a broader coalition in this indispensable battleground.

A similar comparison will become available if socialist Francesca Hong wins Wisconsin's Democratic gubernatorial nomination on Tuesday. While Wisconsin doesn't have a Senate election that could provide a direct benchmark for Hong, she offers a distinct contrast to Josh Shapiro, a centrist (and possible 2028 candidate) who is seeking reelection as governor in Pennsylvania.

To be clear, this isn't only about who can beat their Republican challenger in November. Yes, progressives have much at stake in whether their candidates can win general elections outside deep blue terrain. It's an "all-our-chips on the table moment," says Adam Green, co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, the political organization affiliated with Senator Elizabeth Warren. If El-Sayed (and Hong if she wins the nomination) loses, it will hugely deflate the left. But at a time when Trump's approval has fallen so sharply, each could win without proving that a candidate in their mold can carry their state in a more neutral environment, or with the larger electorate of a presidential election.

That's why the more revealing yardstick in these crucial battlegrounds will be whether the progressive candidates exceed, match, or trail centrists Benson and Shapiro on the November ballot. 

Dan Kanninen, the swing state director for the 2024 campaigns of Joe Biden and Kamala Harris, worries that the progressives are likely to underperform. If that happens, "I just truly hope that those with a particular point of view on policy can confront the realities of the electorate and try to build a coalition that can win" in 2028, he says.

Early general election polling in Michigan has already shown El-Sayed struggling against Republican nominee Mike Rogers among the same key constituencies that largely preferred Representative Haley Stevens in the primary: voters over 50, women without a college degree, and Black voters. In the same poll, Benson was performing at least 15 points better among each of those groups against her Republican opponent, John James.

In Wisconsin, Hong is likely to post huge numbers Tuesday in Dane County - the prosperous, young and well-educated county around Madison. But she could face similar challenges to El-Sayed in both the Black neighborhoods of Milwaukee and the state's midsize cities dominated by working-class White voters. 

Because Democrats have already maxed out in Dane (typically attracting at least 75% of the vote there), Kanninen says the key to winning a Wisconsin general election is improving in those smaller, blue-collar places. "That's the difference between winning by 20,000 votes and losing by 20,000 votes," he says. "And those are not the people clamoring for socialist candidates."

By comparison, Shapiro has demonstrated a much broader appeal in Pennsylvania. During his first election in 2022, he ran slightly better than Democrats typically do among working-class White voters while amassing crushing margins among Black voters and college-educated White voters. Public polling shows Shapiro in position to replicate his performance with all three groups this year.

Finding the right model in Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin is vital for Democrats. Those three states have become the pivot in modern presidential politics. Though not carbon copies, the three are strikingly similar demographically, with more White residents and seniors than the national average, slightly fewer college graduates, and many fewer minorities and immigrants. The trio has voted for the same candidate in all but one presidential election since 1980 - and that candidate tends to win. (The exceptions were the 2000 and 2004 elections, when Democrats Al Gore and John Kerry carried all three but lost to George W. Bush, in Gore's case with an asterisk.) Since 1994, they've even elected governors from the same party in every election but one.

The states converge so deeply that veteran Democratic strategist Tad Devine argues they should be thought of as a single massive swing state - what he calls "Mi-Pa-Wi." Adding Mi-Pa-Wi to the 19 states that have voted against Trump in each of his campaigns, plus Washington DC and Omaha's "blue dot" district, would net the next Democratic nominee exactly the 270 Electoral College votes needed to win.

For that reason, the outcome of the 2026 elections in these states will reverberate loudly. Smart Democrats will study whether the progressive nominees outrun not only their Republican rivals but their centrist counterparts.

news.title: Primaries: Wisconsin Democratiic gubernatorial too close to call
news.text:
Aug. 11 (UPI) -- The race for the Democratic nomination for Wisconsin's governor between democratic socialist Francesca Hong and Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley was too close to call early Wednesday, as primary ballots were being counted in six states.

While primaries were being held in Alabama, Connecticut, Minnesota, South Carolina and Vermont, the Wisconsin gubernatorial race appeared to be a litmus test of whether the Democratic Party's progressive wing was surging across the country after democratic socialist Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan's Democratic Senate primary earlier this month.

The race is being projected as a progressive, Hong, running against a moderate, Crowley, with the possible future of the Democratic Party in play. In the swing state and an open governorship, much is on the line.

Hong, a chef by trade, is the first Asian American member of the Wisconsin Legislature, to which she was elected to in 2022. She's running on a platform that includes a $20 minimum wage indexed to inflation, guaranteed paid leave, fully funded public schools, universal childcare, free school meals and higher taxes on large corporate profits and household income above $1 million a year.

Crowley is running on a moderate platform of affordability and expanding programs already in place, with an emphasize on housing, specifically liberalizing zoning to create houses closer to where people work and converting unused commercial and industrial space into apartments and mixed-use housing. He also supports raising the minimum wage to at least $15 and to $20 by 2030.

The polls closed at 8 p.m. local time.

Late Tuesday, Hong told supporters that while final results have yet to come in she is confident and ready to fight for her vision of Wisconsin.

"We are fighting to become once more what Wisconsin has always been -- a place where our future is determined not by corporations and billionaires, but our future that's determined by the working-class people who live here," she said.

"We fought through this primary because Wisconsinites have rejected the politics of fear, of apathy and division. We are here tonight because thousands and thousands of Wisconsinites across this great state came together in living rooms, in backyards, in bars, in church basements, in community centers, and we came together to demand something new and something better."

The race is for an open governor's mansion as Gov. Tony Evers, a Democrat, decided not to seek a third term.

The winner between Hong and Crowley will go against election denier Rep. Tom Tiffany, a supporter of President Donald Trump, who claimed the GOP nomination Tuesday night over 27-year-old Andy Manske in the two-candidate race.

Tiffany is running on a conservative platform of lowering taxes, a ban on sanctuary jurisdictions and greater accountability for schools.

During his victory speech Tuesday night, Tiffany framed November's election as one about the identity and future of Wisconsin.

"This isn't a typical election about red versus blue; this is an election about the very soul of the state of Wisconsin. It's about what kind of Wisconsin we're going to leave the next generation: Do we pass on a Wisconsin built on freedom -- freedom and opportunity -- or do we accept a future where government gets bigger, taxes keep rising and opportunity becomes harder to find. Because at the heart of this election is a fundamental difference in how we see Wisconsin's future," he said.

In another Democratic race described as progressive vs. moderate, progressive Peggy Flanagan, the lieutenant governor of Minnesota and an Ojibwe activist, claimed the Democratic nomination for Senate over moderate Rep. Angie Craig, who has conceded defeat.

"I am truly honored and humbled to be Minnesota's Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate," Flanagan said in a social media statement.

"Thank you, Minnesota -- for everything."

Unofficial state results show that as of about 11:30 p.m. CDT with nearly 95% of precincts reporting Flanagan had nearly 59% of the vote to Craig's nearly 39.5%.

Flanagan was poised Tuesday night to go against sportscaster and conservative Michele Tafoya, who claimed the GOP nomination for the Senate seat. Unofficial state results show she had 52% of the vote, with Adam Schwarze far behind with 23.76%.

"Minnesota is going 100 miles an hour in the wrong direction after years of single-party rule," she said in a statement after her win. "They've turned our state into a national embarrassment."

They are running for the Senate seat of retiring Sen. Tina Smith, a Democrat who took office in 2018. She endorsed Flanagan to succeed her.

"For now I just want to say how incredibly proud I am of Peggy Flanagan and the people-powered campaign she ran," Smith said in a statement late Tuesday.

In the state's gubernatorial race to replace Gov. Tim Walz, a Democrat, Trump-endorsed Mike Lindell, election denier and MyPillow CEO, was poised to lose the GOP nomination to Lisa Demuth, the Minnesota House speaker.

Unofficial state results show the Lindell-Phillip Parrish ticket won 32.38% of the vote, while the Lisa Deemuth-Ryan Wilson ticket had 43.5%.

On the Democratic side, Sen. Amy Klobuchar, with Ben Schierer as her running mate, was poised for a landslide victory, with unofficial results showing them with nearly 90% of the vote.

"In Minnesota, trust is not given, it's earned," Klobuchar told supporters in claiming victory. "That trust comes with an expectation, which is results -- results that you can see and feel in your life, results in making life more affordable, making our government work and getting rid of the fraud. Results in expanding our economy with a growth agenda. Results that will transform out government and, yes, I will be a transformative governor."

Klobuchar and Demuth are now poised to battle it out for the governor's mansion after Walz ended his campaign for a third term amid incessant attacks from the Trump administration. Trump views Walz as an adversary as he ran as Kamala Harris' running mate in the 2024 presidential election. After Trump returned to the White House, a litany of investigations, probes and reviews were launched into Minnesota from the White House.

news.title: Democrats evenly split in Upper Midwest: Takeaways from Aug. 11 primary
news.text:
Democrats' nationwide tug-of-war between their mainstream liberal and more progressive factions continued Aug. 11 with another neck-and-neck race, this time for the party's nomination in the Wisconsin gubernatorial contest.

With about 93% of the total vote counted, state Rep. Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist ridiculed in the campaign's closing weeks for anti-Thanksgiving posts, held a less than 3,000-vote lead over Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who was backed by party leaders such as Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers.

That marks another significant underperformance by populist outsiders relative to polling − and more proof that the Democratic electorate in key Midwestern swing states is closely divided between its left and center wings − a week after Abdul El-Sayed's razor-thin win over the establishment-backed Rep. Haley Stevens in the Michigan Senate primary.

Speaking to supporters late Tuesday evening, Hong stressed that − no matter who prevails − the Badger State's politics have changed.

"We are fighting to become once more what Wisconsin has always been -- a place where our future is determined not by corporations and billionaires, but our future that's determined by the working-class people who live here," she said.

Progressive did fare better in neighboring Minnesota, where Democratic primary voters handed Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, a progressive, a win over Rep. Angie Craig, a centrist, in campaign to replace retiring Sen. Tina Smith.

That race had many of the same markings as other bitter primaries this year, but was largely shaped by the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, two U.S. citizens, by federal officers in the state earlier this year.

There was also a result that defied polling on the Republican side, as President Donald Trump's near-perfect endorsement record took a hit. Controversy-prone Mike Lindell, the former MyPillow CEO, lost to Minnesota state House Speaker Lisa Demuth in the Republican primary for governor despite having led in polls.

There are also contests Tuesday in Alabama, Connecticut, Vermont and South Carolina, where newly appointed Sen. Darline Graham, the sister of the late Lindsey Graham, who died in July, jockeyed against nine other GOP rivals in a special election.

Here are the key takeaways from Tuesday's election.

Democrats remain evenly split amid liberal, progressive battles

Leading up to Election Day most observers viewed Hong as the favorite given the massive lead she had in many surveys.

But after the polls closed, Hong and Crowley were engaged in an unexpectedly tight contest that underscores how divided Democrats remain over their party's direction heading into the fall.

Many Democrats, including Crowley, spotlighted Hong's stumbles during an Aug. 3 CNN interview that questioned her old social medias posts calling for the cancellation of Thanksgiving.

"She's not ready for prime time," Crowley told USA TODAY.

But others argue those rookie mistakes and previous comments -- including calls to abolish the police -- were eclipsed by Hong's grassroots support and growing frustrations with the party establishment. She galvanized her campaign around universal health care, promises to block data centers and levying higher taxes on the wealthy.

The winner will face Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany, who easily defeated a relatively unknown opponent.

Rematch set for Wisconsin's most competitive district

Further down the Badger State ballot, Democrat Rebecca Cooke is hoping the third time's a charm after easily winning a primary election with the national party's early support.

Rep. Derrick Van Orden is among the most vulnerable Republican incumbents running for re-election amid a projected blue wave that could flip control of the U.S. House of Representatives.

Cooke, a nonprofit owner and former waitress, is hoping that the better political environment will be her edge after failing to get out of the Democratic primary in 2022 and losing to Van Orden by about three percentage points in 2024.

Democratic strategists have noted she outperformed former Vice President Kamala Harris, who lost that district to Trump by about seven percentage points.

Progressives score win in Minnesota Senate primary

Minnesota's Senate primary to replace retiring incumbent Tina Smith was less visible compared to other Democratic primaries this year, but it featured many of the same tensions that gave progressives a decisive win.

Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, cast as the more progressive alternative, was projected as the victor over Rep. Angie Craig, a reliable centrist. The outcome is more remarkable when considering Craig had a roughly $20 million to $4.7 million spending advantage over Flanagan, according to AdImpact.

"For months now, I've been telling you this campaign was about the many versus the money," Flanagan said during her victory speech. "Guess what: The many just won."

The two tussled over the influence of wealthy donors and U.S. support for Israel, while spotlighting support from different wings in the party.

But their race focused mostly on the backlash against the Trump administration's immigration enforcement campaign in the Democratic-leaning state. That resistance culminated earlier this year in the form of massive protests after the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, two U.S. citizens, by federal officers.

Craig argued Flanagan was the preferred opponent for Republicans given her ties to a welfare fraud scandal that ended Gov. Tim Walz’s bid for a third term. The former vice presidential nominee noticeably didn't endorse either contender in this primary.

Federal prosecutors have estimated the fraud in state-run Medicaid programs since 2018 could total more than $9 billion. But Flanagan was relentless in attacking Craig's record, particularly for voting in favor of the Laken Riley Act, an immigration-focused measure that was the first bill Trump signed during his second term.

She will face former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya, who easily won her GOP primary.

Trump ally Mike Lindell loses GOP primary for Minnesota governor

It is rare that GOP voters don't go with President Trump's picks in a primary, but Minnesota Republicans did by rejecting Mike Lindell's bid for governor.

Few MAGA figures have stood by the president as loyally as Lindell, who remains wedded to the false claims that Trump won the 2020 presidential election. The former MyPillow CEO, who stepped down to run for governor, has been held liable for those denials in federal court.

"He will not let you down," Trump said in an Aug. 11 social media post.

Lindell was the frontrunner in most of the surveys leading up to Election Day, but observers began to notice a late surge by Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth. That culminated in her decisive 13-point win over Lindell.

Minnesota's gubernatorial race was always an uphill battle, but Republicans may believe the office is within their grasp, given the welfare fraud scandal in the state.

Demuth is now set to face Sen. Amy Klobuchar, a former presidential candidate who coasted to the Democratic gubernatorial nomination, this fall.

Darline Graham glides to victory -- now comes a bigger run-off test

As expected, Sen. Darline Graham didn't break a sweat in the Aug. 11 primary to replace her late brother, Lindsey Graham, against nine other Republican candidates.

The 62-year-old political newcomer, who was appointed, prevailed carrying about 33% of the vote ahead of well-known names in South Carolina politics including former Gov. Mark Sanford along with Reps. Russell Fry and Ralph Norman.

That margin of victory falls short of the needed 50% threshold to avoid a runoff, however, which means Darline Graham will have to run again on Aug. 25.

Norman, 73, who ran for governor in June, outpaced the other contenders to take second place. He is vice chairman of the House Freedom Caucus that has supported the Trump administration's strict immigration enforcement campaign, but the five-term congressman also endorsed former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley during the 2024 Republican presidential primary.

If things get thorny for Darline Graham against Norman, however, political observers may watch to see if Trump covers his bets by endorsing both candidates, as he did previously during in the state's Republican run-off for governor.

news.title: Ignore the Poll Dancers
news.text:
I don’t know about you, but if you’re statistically like every single one of my conservative friends, you never ever ever ever talk to pollsters.

That’s my personal poll of my friends and acquaintances, a poll with one single question: “Do you ever answer polls?” and the answer is invariably “No,” “Nope,” or “Are you kidding?”

Conservatives just don’t like any of the institutions that have screwed us over the years, and we respond with reasonable hostility. For example, I get calls from the regime media every once in a while asking for a comment, and I tell them flat out, “I don’t talk to the regime media.” I did that to the New York Times not long ago, and up-talking Wellesley grad reportrix on the other end of the line got big mad. Oh well. It just goes to show that we’re done with institutions. They hate us. Hollywood. The media. The pollsters. And we hate them back.

If you look at the pollsters for this November, and if you believe them, things look fairly dire for the GOP and, therefore, America. But if you dig a little deeper, you see a lot of the big-picture polls show that blue areas are really, really, really running up the score for the Democrats, while red areas are much closer but are still red. And some of the results are just flat-out insane. The idea that James Talarico has the lead in Texas doesn’t work for me. I’m going to be in Texas soon in the run-up to the election, and it’s entirely possible that I’ve completely misjudged things, but it’s not likely. There are a lot of libs in Texas because there are a lot of Texans. Still, the idea that a majority of Texans are going to vote for the blasphemous sexually ambiguous creeper who wants to ban guns and hates meat and who looks like he shouldn’t be allowed within 1,000 feet of a kindergarten just doesn’t work.

And last week, the polling didn’t work big-time. 9/11 fanboy Abdul El-Sayed (D-Hamas) was supposed to beat bizarre caricature Haley Stevens (D-Van Down By The River) for the Democrat Senate nomination in Michigan by double digits. He won by barely a digit. That’s a polling miss on par with the infamous 2024 Ann Selzer Iowa poll that had Kamala Harris beating Donald Trump by three and ended up missing by something like 17 points. Some of the polls are so obviously rigged they probably begin with a land acknowledgment.

news.title: Trump says he would like to run for third term, but US laws very strict
news.text:
WASHINGTON, August 12. /TASS/. US leader Donald Trump has stated that he would like to run for a third term as US president, but the country's laws on this matter are very strict.

Trump won the election for the second time in November 2024. He defeated Democratic Party candidate Kamala Harris. He previously headed the US administration from 2017 to 2021.

news.title: Progressive Peggy Flanagan Wins Minnesota’s Senate Democratic Primary
news.text:
WASHINGTON — Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan is projected to win Tuesday’s Democratic primary in Minnesota’s Senate race, defeating Rep. Angie Craig and adding to a streak of victories that progressives are seeing nationwide in primary races against moderates.

Flanagan, who has been Democratic Gov. Tim Walz’s top lieutenant for the past eight years, ran on a message of “the many over the money.” Swearing off corporate PAC money, she traveled the state vowing to champion issues like Medicare for All, a $17 minimum wage hike, affordable housing, restoring Roe v. Wade and fighting political corruption.

Her victory over Craig, a moderate four-term congresswoman who flipped her district from red to blue in 2018, brings an end to their competitive and at times ugly race for the Senate seat currently held by Democrat Tina Smith, who isn’t seeking reelection.

In normal times, this race might have created a fairly predictable divide between the left-leaning and centrist factions of the party. Flanagan had backing from prominent national figures like Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), while Craig was endorsed by moderate Sens. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) and Chris Coons (D-Del.).

But everything went sideways late last year, when the Trump administration flooded Minnesota with Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to purportedly root out criminal undocumented immigrants. Instead, thousands of federal immigration enforcement officers were swarming the state and grabbing Black and brown people off the streets with impunity, regardless of their citizenship status or criminal record.

During their monthslong occupation, ICE agents terrorized immigrant communities, drove families into hiding, circled elementary schools looking for children to nab, violently assaulted peaceful residents and fatally shot two American citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti.

As immigration became a defining issue in their race, Flanagan hammered Craig over her January 2025 vote for the Laken Riley Act, a Republican bill that gave President Donald Trump vast new powers to detain immigrants accused of certain crimes. She also went after Craig over her vote for a GOP resolution last summer condemning an antisemitic attack that included a line expressing gratitude to ICE “for protecting the homeland.”

The attacks stuck. Craig wrote a March op-ed saying she regretted voting for the Laken Riley Act, and tried to turn the tables on Flanagan by loosely tying her to a private prison operator that runs some of ICE’s detention centers. Those attacks didn’t land the same, though.

Tensions rose when Flanagan overwhelmingly won her state party’s endorsement in May, while Craig skipped the nominating convention altogether and said she didn’t want her party’s endorsement anyway, which was nonsense. Her last-minute no-show at the event angered some of the convention’s attendees, including Democratic voters who had turned out to support Craig.

Last month, Craig faced uncomfortable accusations by a prominent Democratic state senator that she sought his endorsement in June 2025 as he was in the ICU after being shot nine times in an attempted assassination. She denied the allegations, which led to the state senator’s wife accusing Craig of lying and spurring an ugly back-and-forth on the matter.

Still, the most astounding aspect of Flanagan’s win is that she overcame an avalanche of outside money being poured into this race to tank her campaign. All told, more than $25 million was spent on this race — with most flowing from pro-Israel and crypto PACs running ads either in support of Craig or attacking Flanagan.

Craig also raised a lot more money than Flanagan. The congresswoman, who did take corporate PAC money, raised $12.7 million as of July 22, compared to Flanagan’s $6.5 million.

“Peggy Flanagan’s win is further proof that the many can beat the money,” Sen. Warren told HuffPost in a statement.

“Voters want leaders with backbones who will stand up to dark money super PACs and fight to make life more affordable,” she said. “I was the very first Senator to endorse Peggy because she’s the fighter we need in Washington.”

Flanagan will take on GOP nominee Michele Tafoya in November and is in a good position to win, as Minnesota hasn’t elected a Republican to the Senate in 20 years. Former Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris, whose running mate was Walz, won this state by more than 4 percentage points in 2024.

If Flanagan does win the general election, she’ll make history as the first Native American woman to serve in the U.S. Senate.

“Peggy Flanagan’s win is further proof that the many can beat the money,” Sen. Warren told HuffPost in a statement.

“Voters want leaders with backbones who will stand up to dark money super PACs and fight to make life more affordable,” she said. “I was the very first Senator to endorse Peggy because she’s the fighter we need in Washington.”

Late Tuesday, Flanagan and Craig presented a united front almost immediately after the race was called, urging their supporters to come together and help Flanagan win the general election in November.

Flanagan will take on Tafoya in November and is in a good position to win, as Minnesota hasn’t elected a Republican to the Senate in 20 years. Former Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris, whose running mate was Walz, won this state by more than 4 percentage points in 2024.

news.title: Minnesota GOP picks Lisa Demuth over Trump-backed Mike Lindell for governor against Democrat Amy Klobuchar
news.text: Minnesota state House Speaker Lisa Demuth won the Republican primary for governor of the state, NBC News projects, defeating Trump ally Mike Lindell and setting up a general election matchup against Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar. Demuth’s primary victory was an upset against Lindell, the MyPillow founder and election conspiracy theorist. Lindell had been leading in limited public polling heading into Election Day and had an endorsement from President Donald Trump. But attacks on Lindell from fellow Republicans — including questions about his residency raised by the chairman of the Minnesota Republican Party — hampered the businessman’s campaign in the final weeks before the primary, as members of the Minnesota GOP sought a nominee who could beat Klobuchar in the general election. Lindell has faced several legal challenges since 2020, when he championed Trump’s debunked theories about the 2020 presidential election, which former President Joe Biden won. At a Minnesota Farmfest forum earlier this month, Klobuchar appeared alongside three GOP candidates for governor and accused them each of being “a rubber stamp of Donald Trump.” But Demuth and other Republicans — including Trump — have attacked Democrats in the blue state over two sprawling fraud scandals involving Medicaid and pandemic aid. The allegations include hundreds of millions of dollars in stolen money that had been earmarked for welfare programs. At the farm event, Demuth blamed “incompetent Democrat control” for the fraud cases, and she has pointed on the campaign trail to the Fraud Prevention Agency Oversight Committee she established while leading the state House. In January, Democratic Gov. Tim Walz, who had planned to run for a third term, decided to drop his re-election campaign, citing the attacks over the fraud cases. A few weeks later, Klobuchar launched her campaign. She is one of four senators to seek the governorship in their home state this year. Still, Republicans will have to overcome political trends in Minnesota in November to win the governor’s mansion. Then-Vice President Kamala Harris won the state by about 4 percentage points in the most recent presidential election, where Walz ran as her running mate.

news.title: Democrat backed by Blue Dogs and Bernie Sanders wins primary as parties prepare to battle for the House
news.text: Tuesday’s primaries are setting the matchups in around a half-dozen competitive House races that will be key to the fight for the House majority in November, including in a hotly contested Democratic target in Wisconsin. Rebecca Cooke won the Democratic primary in Wisconsin’s 3rd District, NBC News projects, and will take on two-term GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden in the fall. The race will be a rematch from 2024, when Cooke lost to Van Orden by about 3 points even though President Donald Trump carried the district by 7 points. A small business owner, Cooke has touted her roots growing up on a dairy farm and tried to eschew political labels, boasting a range of supporters from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee to moderate groups like New Dems and Blue Dogs to a progressive icon in Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt. “I am a Blue Dog and a New Dem, but I’m also very progressive where it counts,” Cooke told NBC News last year. “I don’t like the labels and the boxes that kind of have been created, because immediately, you know, you’re written off and ‘othered’ in your party because you’re this or because you’re that. And really, I’m just — I’m running because I’m for western Wisconsin, period.” Republicans are looking to paint her as too far left for the district. Van Orden campaign spokesperson Grace Kim recently said in a statement that Cook “has aligned herself with the most extreme elements of her party,” pointing to footage of her saying she would support Zohran Mamdani for mayor of New York City and calling for a ban on AR-15 rifles. Cooke has proven to be a strong fundraiser, pulling in nearly $8.6 million to Van Orden’s $7.5 million so far this election cycle. And the race is sure to attract millions more: Super PACs from both parties have already reserved $9 million in airtime for the fall, according to AdImpact. More Democratic targets Democrats also hope they can put another Wisconsin race in play in November: the 1st District in the southeastern corner of the state, where GOP Rep. Bryan Steil is running for a fifth term with Trump’s endorsement. Trump won the district by less than 5 points in 2024. Mitchell Berman, a former nurse at the Department of Veterans Affairs, won the Democratic primary, NBC News projects, after deciding to run for office after the Department of Government Efficiency’s efforts to slash the federal workforce. “I got an email asking me to justify my job,” Berman told the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel. “Give Elon Musk three things that I did in the previous week as an ER nurse at the bedside at the VA. I realized, this is no longer about improving care for veterans.” Berman’s fundraising has lagged behind Steil, who has raised $5.5 million so far this election cycle, while Berman has pulled in $713,000. Democrats are also eyeing Minnesota’s 1st District as a potential pickup, although it is further down the party’s list of targets, given Trump won this seat in southern Minnesota by 12 points in 2024. Trump has endorsed GOP Rep. Brad Finstad in the race. Democrats Jake Johnson and businessman Alex Eaton are competing to take on Finstad in the fall. Republicans go on offense Republicans are looking to pick up Alabama’s 2nd District in the southeastern corner of the state after a redistricting effort redrew the state’s congressional lines. The seat, currently represented by Democrat Shomari Figures, had been one of the state’s largely Black districts, but it shifted towards Republicans after the Supreme Court ruled in June that Alabama could use a different map preferred by state Republicans. In 2024, then-Vice President Kamala Harris had won the old version of the district by 8 points, but Trump would have won it by about 14 points under the new lines. Republicans have nominated state Rep. Rhett Marques, who will take on Figures in the fall. Marques is backed by prominent Republicans including Trump, top members of House GOP leadership and Sen. Katie Britt. Republicans are also looking to make Minnesota’s open 2nd District competitive as they defend the party’s narrow House majority. Trump lost this seat in the Twin Cities suburbs by 6 points in 2024, but it has been a competitive district in recent election cycles. And Democrats no longer have the benefit of incumbency, since Rep. Angie Craig vacated the seat to run for Senate. State Sen. Matt Little won the Democratic primary and will face GOP state Sen. Eric Pratt in the fall.

news.title: Rebecca Cooke, Derrick Van Orden set for rematch in key Wisconsin seat
news.text:
MADISON - Democrat Rebecca Cooke and Republican U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden will square off in a rematch on Nov. 3, after Cooke carried the contested primary in Wisconsin's 3rd Congressional District.

Cooke defeated Eau Claire City Council President Emily Berge, locking in her second race against Republican Van Orden.

Cooke, a nonprofit owner and waitress, is running in the district for the third time. In 2024, she lost to Van Orden in the general election. In 2022, she lost in the Democratic primary.

In 2024, Cooke lost by a narrow margin, coming within less than 3% of Van Orden. She also outperformed then-Vice President Kamala Harris and Democratic U.S. Sen. Tammy Baldwin.

That overperformance is among the reasons Cooke was endorsed by the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee in February this year, allowing her to access campaign resources and staffing in the lead up to the primary.

Berge entered the race last year after being told by national Democratic organizations that they did not want a primary in the 3rd District, and that support would be given to Cooke. Some voters in the district felt the early endorsement of Cooke took away their voice in the primary, instead of providing Cooke a stronger change at defeating Van Orden.

The 3rd Congressional District covers a large portion of the state's Driftless region in the southwestern and western portions of the state. It includes Stevens Point, La Crosse and Eau Claire, as well as some of the Wisconsin areas close to Minnesota's twin cities of Minneapolis and St. Paul.

news.title: CBS Canceled Colbert, But It Still Wants Some Emmy Hardware For His Efforts
news.text:
Despite ending the “Late Show with Stephen Colbert” and firing its host, CBS apparently still wants to take home some hardware during this year’s Emmy Awards. 

On Tuesday, CBS launched a “For Your Consideration” Emmys campaign for the long-running variety program it canceled, citing low ratings and financial difficulties. The network posted an FYC video to the “Late Show’s” official YouTube page on Tuesday, which featured clips of Colbert alongside fellow late-night hosts Jimmy Kimmel, John Oliver, Jon Stewart, David Letterman, Seth Meyers, Jimmy Fallon and Andy Cohen. 

The announcement of Colbert’s termination came just days after the “Late Show” host rebuked the network’s decision to settle a lawsuit with President Donald Trump over a “60 Minutes” interview with former Vice President Kamala Harris. 

Colbert called the $16 million settlement a “big fat bribe.” 

“As someone who has always been a proud employee of this network, I am offended. I don’t know if anything — anything — will repair my trust in this company,” Colbert said. 

CBS contended the show’s cancellation was “purely a financial decision against a challenging backdrop in late night” and was not related “in any way to the show’s performance, content or other matters happening at Paramount.” At the time, CBS’s parent company, Paramount, needed Trump’s FCC to approve a multibillion-dollar merger with Skydance Media.

Colbert’s final show aired on May 17 to an audience of 6.74 million and featured final guest Paul McCartney, who closed the night out with a performance of the Beatles’ song “Hello, Goodbye.” 

Also nominated in this year’s new Outstanding Variety Series category, which merged the old Outstanding Talk Series and Outstanding Scripted Variety Series categories, were “Jimmy Kimmel Live!,” “The Daily Show,” “Last Week Tonight with John Oliver” and “Saturday Night Live.” 

Kimmel, for his part, made clear who he was supporting for this year’s award when he erected a billboard in West Hollywood that read “I’m Voting For Stephen” alongside his own show’s Emmy campaign ad.
